In this fair stranger's eyes of gray, Thine eyes, my love! I see. I shiver; for the passing day Had borne me far frr m thee. This is the curse of life! That not A nobler, calmer train Of wiser thoughts and feelings blot Our passions from our brain, But each day brings its petty dust Our soon-choked souls to fill; And we forget because we must, And not because we will. MATTHEW ARNOLD.

A Hoetow MOClCERY.—Mistress (arranging for dinner) : "Didn't the macareni come from the grocer's, Bridget?" Bridget: " Yis, mum, hut Oi tint it back. Ivery wan av thim stims was impty." Little Willie stood watching his mother, who WAS fill- ing a lamp one morning with very clear oil. Suddenly the little fellow asked: "Is that water your are putting in the lamp. mamma?" Why, no, child, water won't burn." Quick came the answer: "Hot water will, though." The late Dr. Graham was a notorious punster. On one occasion Mr. W. S. Caine. at a dinner-table, defied any one to make a new pun on his name, offering to give five shillings as a reward to any local charity. Dr. Graham at once replied, "Don't be in a hurry-Caine; hand over the two half-crowns." Travelling in a second-class carriage a gentleman had a little misunderstanding with a lady, the only occupant of the compartment besides himself, with reference to the opening of a window. "You don't appear to know the difference between the second and third class," said the lade.- cuttingly. "Oh, madam," replied he, "I am an old railway traveller: I know the class distinctions. In the first class the passengers behave rudely to the guards; in the third the guards behave rudely to the passengers; in the second "—with a bow to his fellow passenger— "the passengers behave rudely to each other." JAPANESE FOOT-GEAR.—in Japan. children's shoes are made of blocks of wood secured with cords. The 'stock- ing resembles a mitten, having a separate place for the great toe. As these shoes are lifted only ho the t OP?, the heels make a rattling sound as their owners walk, which is quite stunning in a crowd. They are not worn in the house, as they would injure the soft straw mats on the floor. You leave your shoes at the. door. Every house is built with reterence to the number of mats required for the floors, each room having from eight to sixteen; and in /eking lodgings, you pay so mach for a mat. They think it extravagant, in us to require a whole room to ourselves. The Japanese shoe gives perfect freedom to the foot. The beauty of the human foot is only seen in .the Japanese. They haxe no corns, no ingrowing nails, no distorted joints. Our toes are cramped until they are deformed, and are in danger of extinction. They have the full use of their toes, and to them they are almost like fingers. Nearly every mechanic makes use of his toes in holding his work. Every toe is fully developed. Their shoes cost a penny, and lasts six months. A NEW WAY TO GET A LEGACY.—An Old resident of Buffalo, New York, sick in bed and likely to die, sent for a lawyer to make his will, that he might dispose of his life-long earnings and savings. He told the attorney that he had 30,000 dole., and proceeded to dictate his dispositions. To his wife be gave 15,000 do's., and 5,000 dols. to each of his three children. These bequests were ' to be first paid, and then he went on to dispose of the ! residue. "Considering the love and affection that I bear to my beloved nephew John, I give and bequeath to him 5.0c0 dole. Considering the love and affection that I bear to my two nieces Sally and Polly, I give to7each of them 5,000 dols." And he was going on, when the law- yer laid down his pen and remarked, "This seems to me a work of supererogation." "What do you mean," in- quired the testator, surprised at the remark. "Why." said thil lawyer, " you say yourself that you have lint 30,000 dols., and you have given all that to your wife and children; and I was thinking that if you have nothing more, hut are willing 5,000 dials. apiece to your beloved nephews and nieces, why, I don't see how they _ are going to get it." The' old man was nettled; his eyes showed some fire, notwithstanding his weak state, as he answered. "Git ? llow're they goin' to it it? Why, dog on 'ens! let 'em work for it, as I had to do." The Uses OF THE MOSQUITO.—A gentleman in Madras has had the courage to say a good word for the Mos- quito. This insect is a waist, and its hite is a great deal ' worse than its buzz, and that is had enough. Fortu- nately for some of us the mosquito cares only for the warmer parts of the globe. I won't call the Madras naturalist the mosquito's champion, because he doesn't ignore its evil ways, but he urges that we should not lose sight of the useful services which the insect, renders to man in an earlier stage of its existence. Putting the life of the mosquito at 29 or 30 days, he points out that three of these days are spent in the egg form, that no ' fewer than 21 are given over to the larval form, two days are occupied by the chrysalis and only three or four by the winged form in which all the biting mischief is done. Now during the egg and pupa (or chrysalis) stares the createre is idle, but how is the larva engaged for the three weeks of its existence? Its home is the foulest stagnant water, and its food decayed vegetable and animal matter, on which it feeds voraciously. Thus the whole of its energy is displayed in purifying filthy water. Why, asks the Madras champion, who is not a champion, should not 21 days of hard and useful labour outweigh the stings of three or four days? But perhaps he has never had a bite.—Litile Folk, Magazinefor Jane.' Dicxrxs's iIAvENS.—TI-1,9 original of Grip the Raven, as every one knows, was in Dickens's possession for a . considerable time, and its death was a domestic cala- mites The famous bird was replaced by another, older, and lareer Grip, so that " Barnaby" should have the fruit of contineal study of the habits of ravens, but he also met with an untimely end. "The first," says Dickens. "was in the bloom of his youth, when he as discovered in a modest retirement in London, by a friend of mine, and given to me. . . . He slept in a stable, generally on horseback," and "was rapidly rising in acquirements and virtues, when, in an evil hour, his stable was newly painted. He observed the workmen closely, saw that they were careftd of the paint, and immediately burned to possess it. On their going to dinner, he ate up all they had left behind, consisting of a pound or two of white lead: and this youthful indiscretion terminated in death. While I was yet unconsolable for his loss, another friend of mine in Yorkshire discovered an older and more - gifted raven at a villosse public-house, which he prevailed upon the landlord to part with for a consideration, and sent up to me." After describing the merits and eccen- tricities of this bird, Dicke& wrote: "It mar have been that he was too bright, a genius to live long, or it may have been that he took some pernicious substance into his bill, and thence into his maw, which is not impro- bable, seeing that he new-pointed the greater part of the garden-wall by digging out the mortar, broke countless squares of glass by scraping away the putty all round the fmmes, and tore up andswallowed, in splinters, the greater part of a wooden staircase of six steps and a landing, but after some three years he too was taken ill, and died before the kitchen fire. He kept his eye to the last upon the meat as it roasted, and suddenly turned over on his back with a sepalchral cry of 'Cuckoo!'" The remains of Grip the First were stuffed and sent home in a glees case, by way of ornament to his master's study, and some years afterwards were sold by public auction for the fancy price of £l2o.—Temple Bar. AMERICAN LOCOMOTIVES : WHY THEY ARE THE BEST,— The key to the evolution of the American railway is the contempt for authority displayed by our engineers, and the untrammelled way in which they invented and ap- plied, whatever they thought would answer the best pur- po%e, regardless of precedent. When we began to build our railways. in 1831. we followed English patterns for a short time. Our engineers soon saw that unless vital changes were made our money would not hold out, and our railway system would be very short. Neces- sity truly became the mether of invention. The first, and most far reaching, invention was that of the swivelling truck, which, placed under the front end of an engine, enables it to run around curves of almost any radius. This enabled us to build much less expensive lines than those of England, for we could now curve around and avoid hills and other obstacles at will. The next improve- ment was the invention of the equalising beams or levers, by which the weight of the engine is always borne by three out of four or more driving-wheels. They act like a three-legged stool, which can always be set level on any irregular spot. The original imported English locomotives could not be kept on the rails of rough tracks. The same experience obtained in Canada when the Grand Trunk Railway was opened, in 1854-55. The locomotives of English pattern constantly ran off the track; those of American pattern hardly ever did so. Finally. all their locomotives were changed by having swivelling trucks put under their forward ends, and no more trouble occurred. The equalising levers were first used by Rogers, in 1844. These two improvements, which are absolutely essential to the success of railways in new countries, and have been adopted in Canada, Australia, Mexico, end South America, to the exclusion of Englisn patterns, are also of great value on the smoothest and best possible tracks. The flexibility of the American machine increases its adhesion and enables it to draw greater loads than its English riVal. The same flexibility equalises its pressure on the track. prevents Shocks and blows, and enables it to keep out of the hospital and run more miles in a year than an English locomotive.—Scribner's J'lagazine. THE WILD WEST. By Sion.
(From the "Blackburn Time')

Since being a small boy I have been a consistent ad- mirer of the noble red man, as pourtrayed by Captain Mayne Reid and J. Fennimore Cooper. He has always been my beau ideal of Nature's nobleman. Could any- thing have been more chivalric than the conduct of Oceola in "The Last of the Mohicans ?" Not to my boyish idea at anyrate. I have pictured him in my mind's eye, with his stoical indifference to circumstances and his heroic form and picturesque dress. I was greatly troubled that he was the last of his race, because I thought that all his race would naturally be of his pattern, full of poetic motion and sentiment, brave as lions, yet gentle as lambs. He and the other Indians of the novels of those writers were no imaginary charac- ters to me; no, they really existed, and those of them who bad not fallen beneath the unerring rifle of Bill Biddon, the celebrated trapper, or of Hawkeye, the famous scout, and others of their kidney, were still living realities. Such of them as the scouts and trappers designated varmint and pesky redskins I looked upon with their eyes, and felt glad every time their deadly rifles "spoke" and dropped one. And what unerring eyes, and ears, and judgment those wonderful scouts and trappers had. They actually knew the voices of each others' rifles. A footprint in the grass, a broken twig, a piece of bark knocked off a tree, or the remnants of a camp fire, were a whole chapter of a book to them. Wonderful men those plainsmen for by any of those simple signs they could guage the locatiOn of the pesky varmint to a mile. They were veritable sleuth-hounds I were those men, for, if once they got upon the track of an Indian, or a band of Indians, who had incurred their resentment,thatlndian or that band was aoomed. Then the high-flown rhetoric of those noble redmen. It was much akin to the stilted verbosity of the ancient Greeks and Romans. only more so; and yet so simple and pathetic. I was very, sorry that it was necessary to drive them to- wards the setting sun. I read that they were being rapidly decimated by their palefaced foes, and nit the race would eventually become extinct, and I sympathised with them. I had always felt a desire to see one of them, but never thought that that was within the bounds of possibility until I read that Buffalo Bill's Wild West Show was coming to England ; then I felt that I was about to have the chance of gratifying one of.the wishes of a lifetime Still I could hardly realise that Buffalo Bill would bring bona fide samples of the noble Chingackgook and Napanogock. It seemed at first to be too good news to be true, but, when I read a more de- tailed account of the show, and found that the celebra- ted Red Shirt, and Sitting Bull, with other chiefs, were members of the company I believed that I was to have my wish gratified by gazing upon the dusky forms of real live Indians, who had swung the deadly tomahawk and lifted ha'r.

..... I curbed my impatience until the Wild West came to Manchester, and waited a few weeks until I thought the crush would be over, and then, one Thursday at noon, I speculated two shillings in a railway ticket, and took a seat in a train bound for the city of cotton, with the in- tention of seeing Buffalo Bill with his troop of Indians, cowboys, and other western notabilities. When I took my seat in the train, I did so next to an acquaintance, a retired photographer, who was going to Manchester to see an opera by Carl Rosa's Company. Pacing me, on the other seat, was an individual in a shabby silk hat and frock coat. He was tall and thin, and had a jaundiced look about his face and eyes that gave him the appearance of one who was not enjoying life, and who looked upon it as a vale of tears through which he was helplessly wading. His inside coat pocket was full of religious tracts, and he had some more in a small satchel, which he had on his knee. Between his knees he had a large alpaca umbrella, with a big dis- coloured knob, upon Which he placed his hands, but not as other people do, for the sake of ease, but, as it ap- peared to me, to add dignity to his pose, for he did not lean any weight upon his umbrella, but sat bolt up- right, like a China figure, and looked as mournful as a picture of a deceased saint. Now, there is a something in the demeanour of indi- viduals of this class of religious monomaniacs that grates on my nerves and irritates me, as I often think, myself, unreasonably. There is an assumption of superiority and smugness in their very word and action that rouses one's gall. Their every manner of speaking to you convinces you that they feel they have passed through the chastenhkg fires, and that you are still waltzing in the paths of wickedness, and are there- fore deserving of their pity ; which said pity they allow to slop over until you are besplattered with a coating of it as thick as an elephant's hide. Then there is such a nice blending of condescension with the pity that, if you are of a sensitive and a resentful nature, you feel your gorge rising within you, anti presently it slops over too. I have met with so many. persons of this class in my chequered career that I have become Cal- lous, I am afraid, and not easily appalled, by the future terrors these fulminators of heaven's thunder- bolts flying about so recklessly, and with such lavish wastefulness. I feel sure that, from the way in which they deal them out, there will not be sufficient to go round, but still I hope for the best—l do not mean the best thunderbolt. There was in the corner of the compartment, and next to me on my right, a man who, from his garb and ap- pearance, I took to be a bobbin-carrier in a factory, or something of that sort. He was small in stature, round- shouldered, and sat in a rather crouching position. Like the class of persons who generally occupy the inferior situations in a mill, he did not look over- burdened with intelligence. But he seemed to be of a nervous and restless temperament, and he jerked his head and his little beady eyes about in all directions. While I was having a few words with my acquaintance, the photographer, I noticed that a conversation was being started between this little chap and the tract man, though I was not exactly watching them. Just as the train was slowly drawing itself out of the station we were all in the com- partment a little startled by hearing the man of tracts say to the corner man in a voice that would have been worth a fortune. to. tragedist, and which somehow re-

minded me of Clapham cave. - "My friend, are you saved ?" Such a question in a railway train, and in such a tone of voice at once, arrested the attention ot evecy person •in the compartment, of whom there were eight, includ- ing the speaker. As I had previously had the same conundrum propounded to me, and as it had been a bit of a doorer to me, I wondered how our friend in the corner would hop out of the difficulty, and how he would reply. Ile looked the tract man full in the face in a dazed sort of a way for a second or two, and then snapped out:
• WOrni ?" "I asked you, my friend, in all sincerity, Axe you saved ?" said the tract man.

The man still gazed at him for another second, and then a light seemed to dawn upon him, for his features relaxed, and a faint smile overspread his countenance, and ma tone that showed he was pleased at the interest taken in him by a stranger, he replied; "Oh aye, aye, awm reet enough neaw. But id were a job aw con tell yo "Was it ?" said the tract man. "I'm glad to hear that you overcame the enemy. Did you have a mighty struggle with him, my friend ?" . . .

"Mighty struggle! Mighty struggle! Aw should think aw dud hey a mighty struggle! Yo'd a thowt SOO4 iv yo'd a bin i' my place." "Then you were very nearly overcome?- " Varra near o'ercorne! Aw shrink] think aw wor. Wey, t' docther hissel sed as it my hedn'd tekken a change at twelve o' t' clock at fleet aw should a bin a deead mon!! -

"Then you were brought to a sense of your condition while you were on a bed of sickness?' "Sense o' condition! There were no sense o' condi- tion abeawt mo, aw can tell yo; asvd no sense at o. Befoor awd bin i' t' feyver four days mi sense o' went. un aw were unshonscions ; un t' wost o' t' job were o'er when aw coorn to in sense o' condition, as yo' CO'fl id." The man of tracts was getting the worst of the con- versation, and after the man's last speech he looked a bit confused, because he could see that everybody in the compartment was listening to and was amused by the corner man's answers. Whether his answers were given designedly or whether he was as innocent as be looked, I could not determine, but in either case it was a treat,

-to help the& to a better understanding of each other. After the tract man had pulled himself together a bit, he said: *I do not think you understand me, my friend. What I wish to ask you is: Have you ever sought and found salvation?"

• Whether the man was innocent or not when he replied I cannot say, but he said. "Nay, aw corn'd say as aw've fun owt o' thad sooart, but aw corn'n see as weel as aw use to could, un aw've happen missed id wi' bein' a bit near-seeted."

The man of tracts preached a short homily to the corner man, in which he pointed out the danger he was in of being consigned to the lake of fire if he did not live in such a manner as would qualify him for the better land. Just as the train began to slow for Darwen, the man in the corner said, "Well, suppooase aw dorn'd live quite as aw should do, wod will they do wi' mo when aw dee?"

"You will go to the lake of brimstone and fire." " Wod, ml body ?" "Oh, no; they will bury that." "Well, if they'll tek ml body to t' churchyard un bury id, ther welcome to do owt as they'n a mind wi' owt as is left. They'll nod find so much owd butty, will they, think'st ta ?" said the man, as he was getting out, and chuckling to himself as he walked along the platform at Darwen Station.

The amusement that everybody showed damped the ardour of the tract man, and after that he maintained a stolid silence until we got to Bolton, where he got out. There is in this world nothing more beautiful than religion. Its benign .effects are not equalled by the teachings of any code of morals, but I do think it pos- sible to obtrude it at the wrong time and in the wrong place. And I believe that a teacher may be so unfitted to disseminate its principles and its virtues that he may do more harm than good by assuming an office for which he has no qualifications. We arrived in Manchester about three o'clock. After leaving the photographer in Market-street, I called upon two friends, who agreed to go with me to the Wild West if I would stay tea with them first. This suiting my arrangements to a " t"—l mean tea—l fell in with the idea. At half-past five the three of us were perched on the top of a 'bus in Deansgate waiting to be wafted west- wards—that is, if the Wild West lay in that direction. My two friends, Joe and Ted, had pioneered me through the streets and entries, and round corners and through courts, and through the crowds of pedestrians, to that 'bus in a manner that was truly wonderful. While they were slipping through the crowds like greased eels I was apologising to about every sixth person for jolting him. I did get to the 'bus without really knocking anybody down, but I had to clasp one old lady very affectionately in my arms to save her. She might have saved her tongue afterwards,.but she preferred not to. I left her . . .

with her umbrella held up in a threatening manner. It is a wonderful performance, too, in my opinion, is driving a 'bus along those thoroughfares. Our driver was an adept both at driving and in speaking to other drivers in blassical language. He could make the eh, enmainbient air fairly twitch and assume a blue strip*, appearance that was beautiful to look upon—if one ad- mired that kind of thing. But he didn't corrupt the morals of the police officers by using that kind of language in their hearing. (To be concluded next week.)

FROM LONDON LETTERS Scc _— Mr. Bright's three sans are in London, but though they confirm the general news as to the favourable progress' of their father's recovery, it is not at all likely that Mr. Bright will take any Tart in the work of the House of Commons for this session; and as he has never, I believe, entered the house since the opening in February, this session will for him in this respect resemble that of about thirty years ago, when Mr. Bright suffered the illness from which Cobden at onetime feared his energy would not recover.

A dirty old Portrait of Robert Burns was recently bought at a broker's shop in Toronto for £2. It has been carefully cleaned, and turns out to be an oil painting by Raeburn, dated 1787. The purchaser now values it at £2.000, and he intends to send it to Scotland for exhibition, with a view to its sale. This picture was bought many years ago at the sale of the household effects of a deceased Scotch farmer in Canada. There are stories afloat that the DoWliger-Coun- tess of Dudley is to be married before long to a French nobleman. The report is hardly credible, for the simple reason that long ago Lady Dudley and Lord Rowtoa were believed to have something more than a passin.: interest in one another. Ills lordship is still a bachelor, and if he allows the French nobleman to carry off Lady Dudley from these shores it will surprise very much those people who are best acquainted with the facts. Lord James Douglas.loves not wisely, if too well, and he has gone to prison for communicating with a ward in Chancery after Chancery had forbidden him to hold any intercouse with its ward. So far so good. But I think that the judge somewhat exaggerated when he said that the Christmas card that Lord James sent to the ward was one which no gentleman would send to a lady. It represents a little child asleep, with two small elves half-hid- den behind a fence and peeping at the child. One is holding a wheat-stalk in his hand and tickling the child's face, with the intention, I suppose, of awakening it. Long before the weak-kneed speech of Mr. Rit- chie on Tuesday it was understood that Sir H. James is to have his triumph, and that the ex- Attorney-General of the Liberals is to have the honour of making Bury and all towns of 50,000 population exceptions to the rule and authority of the General County Councils. The change, if it be conceded, is important, because the aim of those who desire the largest possible measure of local government has been to clothe the County Councils with great powers, and this policy will becorde the snore questionable when for the purposes of the I Act a county may be defined as a borough not even I orthe second class.

_ If the "intelligent foreigner" had seen Mr. Par- nell on Wednesday afternoon in Hyde Park, his , bridle resting loosely on his horse's neck, his own attitude and face suggesting an irreducible mini- , mum of activity, he would have wondered that this sauntering in could be the wary and unfail- ing leader n the most angry controversy; and yet then can be no doubt that Mr. Parnell is almost an ideal leader in the present circumstances of Ireland. Sir Lepel Griffin used without acknowledgment the other night the opinion of a very great .statesman of the past that courage was the first and the second quality in a political leader, and this fearless sense of responsibility Mr. Parnell possesses in a singular degtee. It needs only a moment's reflection to be aware how inconvenient a more impulsive man, one over-fond of the show and glitter of leadership, would be in the position which Mr. Parnell occu- pies with so mrch discretion and dignity. The opposition raised by Mr. Justice Stephen to the liberation of the press from an absurd and op- pressive law of libel—a law which makes a pro- prietor or an editor criminally responsible for giv- ing faithful reports of public meetings—has com- pletely broken down. The House of Commons on ' Wednesday accepted in detail the more important I principles of the Libel Law Amendment Bill, and rejected the advice of lawyers, who ought to know better, founded upon a belief that the great object of a journalist is to defame private character. The II bill was carried through committee up to its fifth clause, and the operation of the new rules which give its precedence on the orders of the day over all other measures when Government business does not intervene, will enable it to be carried to the statute book. The intervention of Mr. Justice Stephen was entirely gratuitous, and his criticisms were founded upon a misapprehension. But the one good objec- tion lie made has been met by an amendment, and the bill as it is likely to pass will fairly satisfy the demands which , hays been made by the Fourth Estate. The first business was the consideration of the annual report and balance sheet. The report stated that of 36 matches played 17 had been won, 10 lost, and nine drawn, and many of the engagements had been with clubs of the highest standing in the Rugby Union. The following players had scored for the first team :—J. Jol- ley, two dropped goals and nine tries; J. T. Massey, four dropped goals and fair tries; T. Barnes, five dropped goals, and one try; W. Bandies and Frank Turner, four tries each; W. Speakman, R. Littlewood, W. Povey, and T. Davies three tries each; J. E. Warren and Fair. Turner, two tries each • J. Appleton, W. Daniels, H. Ashton, W. Dillon, E. Dillon; and W. Antro- bus, one try each. Out of 24 matches the" A" team had won 17, drawn 3, and lost 4. The followingplayers scored: ' J. W. Evans, 5 dropped goals, and 11 tries; j. Appleton, 1 dropped goal and 10 tries; J. Whittle, W. Antrobus, Isherwood, and Daniels, 4 tries each ; W. Bandies and Sanson, 3 tries ; L Cragan, H. Boardman, J. Hackett, W. Molyneaux, W. Eyes, W. Nevins, J. Bate, and J. Law- less, 2 tries each; J. T. 'Thornley, Jones, W. Speakman, T. Barnes, and R. Littlewood, 1 try each. J. Isherwood had placed 15 goals from tries, T. Walsh 2, J. Appleton 2, T. Barnes, 2, and T. Jolley 1, The second team had won 13 matches, drawn 6, and lost 2. The following players scored :—J. Lawless, 8 tries; C. Unsworth, 7 tries; S. Mather, 6 tries; J. T. Bate; 4 tries ;W. War- burton, 11. Boardtnan, W. Nield, T. Bibby, and G. Rat- cliffe, 2 tries each ;F. Bate, Cl. Beard, J. Warburton, J. Actot , Coytfe, J. Boyle; Slater, Russell, and Jefferson, 1 try each. There' had been a large increase in• the number of members. 153 had joined since the last general meeting, making the total number of members now 70 honorary and 316 ordinary. Matches had been arranged with the following clubs for next season :—Tyldesley. Rochdale Hornets, Free Wanderers, Oldham, Coven- try, Broughton Rangers, Wigan, Kendal Hornets, Wakefield Trinity, Barrow, Moseley (Birmingham), Broughton. Mossley, Leeds Parish Church, Rugby. The balance sheet showed that £955s 5d had been paid to various clubs as share of gate money; £42 16s 7d had been expended on jerseys, caps, and bas; and £lB 2s 9d on boots, shin-guards, Szc. The cost of dinners and refreshments to committee, players, and visiting teams amounted to £99 9s Id, and hotel expenses to £6O 13s 7d The new ground, pavilion, and other alterations and im- provements had cost V 39 Os 2d; and the sum of £ll9 12s 2d had been spent in railway fares. The total ex- penditure was £1,234 18s 4d. The receipts included £B5O 14s Oid gate money, and £l2O 13s 6d received as entratre fees and subscriptions. There was a balance , due to treasurer of £3O 17s 7d, less £1 12s 4cl cash in bank. The assets totalled £313 12s 41, including £3OO, the estimated value of stock. On the annual ball there was a profit of £5 19s 2d. In connection with the junior football competition in aid of local charities, the follow- ing contributions had been made to such institutions : Infirmary £lO, Ladies Charity £lO. children of Flamil- ton-st. Schools, £2 lOs Od, and Workhouse Schools, Pad- gate, £2 lOs Od. These matches realised £B6 4s Od in gate money, and £26 5s pa was expended on medals.—A short discussion took place in regard to the report and balance sheet, and, in answer to questions, Mr. Pember- ton said that in the course of the, year £B5O had been taken in gate money. The stock had been valued at what it was thought it would fetch if brought to the hammer. He must decline to say anything about the hotel expenses, for which receipts had been produced. There were between 70 and 80 playing members.—Mr. WARREN mentioned that there had been an idea of form- ing a gymnasium and reading room for the club, and they had been on the look out for suitable premises. The room that the committee had taken on Friar's-green was adapted for a reading room, and there was a morn that would do for boxing, dumb-bell, and Indian club exer- cise. There had been some idea Of getting the back premises for a gymnasium, but it had fallen through, and it was possible that the premises would be required by the Corporation, and would have to be given up. Very little expense had been incurred in this matter.— The report and balance sheet were then adopted, on the motion of Mr. J. L. WHITTLE, seconded by Mr. S. Aser- NALL.

div.head: ELECTION OF PRESIDENT.
div.p: ELECTION OF PRESIDENT.

The retiring president of the club (Councillor W. Pier- point) was re-elected president for the ensuing year, Councillor Tinsley presiding over the meeting while the election took place.—Councillor W. PIERPOINT, on re- suming the chair, was very heartily applauded. He thanked the members of the club for the honour they had done him for the second time in electing him president of their club. He had listened with a very great deal of pleasure to the questions with reference to the balance sheet, and he thought that balance sheet was a very good one taking the figures on both sides. They had in War- rington an excellent club which played excellent games, and played football as it ought to be played ; and as a consequence they had had the sympathies of the people of Warrington, and that being so they had had a large amount of following and had taken enormous gates. He had no doubt that next year the play would be even better than in the past, and in all probability their gate money would be greater. (Hear, hear.) He tuggested therefore that it would be desirable to get a very heavy reserve fund for the club. (Applause.) They might have a series of bad years, but then if they were pro- vided in their good times they were able to stand the 'dad times when they came. Their Club was well managed, their players played well, their commit- tee attended to its work, they had an exceedingly good secretary and treasurer, and their accounts were beauti- fully kept. He did not think any exception could be taken to the work done by the secretary and treasurer. (Hear, hear.) He should like to impress upon the in- coming committee the desirability of practising economy in every single particular. If they had economy ana

If the following, among the world's distinguished ones, live to celebrate their respective birthdays this year, Bismark will turn 73. Verdi will be 84, John Bright will be 77, Adelaide Ristori will turn 67, Edwin Booth will be 55, Wilkie Collins, Professor Huxley. and the Emperor Dom Pedro will be 63; Meissonier, the painter, will have lived just three- quarters of a century; Gladstone, Oliver Wendell Holmes, and Alfred Tennyson will be 79; Ferdinand de Lesseps, the French engineer, will reach 83; George Bancroft, the American historian, and Von Moltke, the German warrior, will be 88—as old as the century; Queen Victoria and John Ruskin will score 69 summers; the spirit of 70 will animate Robert Browning and Harriet Beecher Stowe; threescore and ten will number the years of Gounod and James Anthony Fronde; Mark Twain will be 52, Bret Harte 49, the prince of Wales 47, and Adelina Patti 45.

In accordance with usage when subjects such as that which occupied the attention of the House of Commons on Tuesday evening are discussed, the Speaker closed the section of the Ladies' Gallery which is under th e direct patronage of Mrs. Peel. The Speaker has no authority to prohibit ingress to the other portion of the gallery at the disposal of pri- vate members who have obtained precedence at the ballot-box, but he took a step which, as far as the ordinary class of visitants to this part of the House is concerned, effectually closed the doors. He caused it to be intimated to whomsoever might ap- ply for admission that the subject of debate was of a character not suitable to the hearing of ladies. This message, delivered by the courteous atten- dant, proved effectual in some cases, ladies hastily turning tail and vanishing; but at least fourteen ladies, some with names not unfamiliar in platform controversy, and most of them unmarried, insisted upon their right to enter, and, no objection being offered, sat through the debate. There is a son of the Russian Grand Duke Con- stantine at present living in Turkestan in exile. His story is an interesting one. He is said to be en- dowed with great natural gifts; but in youth he turned out badly. Some twelve years ago, when about twenty-five years old, he fell under the influ- ence of an unfcrtunate passion for an American beauty of the demi-monde, and appropriated some very valuable jewels belonging to his mother which she had used to decorate ' the image of a saint in the palace chapel. The act was looked upon with holy horror, and ruined the young Grand Duke's career. He lost his title, all his rights, and is now residing in Turkestan under the name of Nicholas Romanof, this being the family name of the Imperial reigning house. At the place where he now -re Sides he shows great energy, and devotes his time .and talents to the development of local weilth. He owns a large silk factory, which is doing an excellent business. He has turned his attention to irrigation, and in other ways is doing good to the country of his adoption. He is ve7 much liked, and perhaps one day he may regain his lost title and position.

Pierpoint, and amongst those also present were Councillors Tinsley and Fleming, and Messrs. J. L. Whittle, T. Dinwiddie, J. Evans, D. Tinnion, J. Hedgecock. W. Howard, C. R. Adamson, J. E. Warren (hou. sec.), and T. Pember- ton (hon. tress).

at." 47- "••1:- good play combined he-nad rin doubt that they should have a very good reserve 'fund. The stock had been taken as very much below its value, and he didnot think anybody but a football club could afferd to value their stock on so low a scale as they had done. (Applause.) ELECTION OF OFFICERS. The PRESIDENT mentioned that as there was no oppo- sition in the case of the Hon. Secretary (Mr. J. E. War- ren), and Hon. Treasurer (Mr. T. Pemberton), those two gentlemen were re-elected for the coming year. (Ap- plause.)—Four candidates had been nominated as audi- tors, two of whom were required. On 'a vote being taken Mr. C. R. Adamson and Mr. F. Webster were de- clared elected, but as Mr. Adamson withdrew, Mr W. Bibby, who received the next highest number of votes, was substituted. As captain of the first team Mr. W. Dillon was erected unopposed, and in returning thanlcs said he should think a lot of the position they had elec- ted him to, and do his very utmost to bring the team to success right through the season. (Applause.)—Of the two nominees for the post of vide-captain of first team, Mr. W. Speakman was elected.—Mr. J. T. Whittle was re-elected captain of the "A " team, and Mr. W. Antro- bus as vice-captain of the same team.—Captaincy of second team, two candidates, Mr. J. "T. Bate elected: sub-captain of same team, two candidates, Mr. J. H. Lawless elected.—Mr. J. Archer was re-elected reporter of the first team, and Mr. G. Hill was appointed to a similar office for the "A" team.—For the post of umpire of the first team there were five candidates, one of whom (Mr. T. Barnes, senr.,) however, withdrew. Out of the others Mr. 'l'. Davies was elected. Mr.- S. Wright was re-elected umpire of the'A team, out of four candidates. —Of the two candidates for the place of umpire of the 2nd team Mr. J. Holmes was elected.

div.head: BLICTION. OF COMMITTEE AND TRUSTEES.
div.p: BLICTION. OF COMMITTEE AND TRUSTEES.

There were thirty-two candidates nominated for elec- tion to the committee, but as some of those nominated had been previously elected to other offices, a number of names were withdrawn. Eight committee men were I balloted for, and the following were he successful can- didates, the names being given in the order read out by I the president, and not accordinz to the number of votes received by each, viz.:—Messrs Adamson, G. Smith, E. Gilbert, H. Ashton, J. Evans, J. L. Whittle, W. H. Dut- ton, and Fair. Turner.—Messrs J. Evans and G. Smith were also elected trustees. THE WEST LANCASHIRE COMPETITION.

Mr. FAIR. TURNER moved "That the Warrington Foot- ball Club enter for the West Lancashire Cup Competi- tion next season." The first reason, he said, for propos- ing the motion was that by entering the competition they would increase the interest in football in Warring- ton; the second was that they would now get the semi- final gate, which they did not before; and besides, there was a lot of young blood in the club which might wish to compete next season. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. T. BARNES seconded the proposal.—The Holy. Sac. said the dates on which they would have to play the cup ties next seaso-4 were all filled up with the Broughton Rangers, the Man- chester Rangers, the Kendal Hornets, and the Free 'Wanderers, and if they went in for the cup the only honourable way to do was to give these clubs notice at once. He should have thought that they had had plenty of the cup in the past they had never found it advanta- geous or any way else. (Hear, hear.) He also men- tioned that at a meeting of the. West Lancashire Com- mittee it had been decided to distribute £6O to charities, £l5 of which was to be given to Widnes, £l5 to St. Helens, £l5 to Wigan, and only £5 to Warrington. (" Oh, oh," and "Shame.") _ After all they had done for the ;hit= he thought that was intended as a slight. (Hear, hear.)--On being put to the Vote the motion wis` negatived by a large majority.

- THE- SECOND TEAM CAPTAIN. Mr. J. LAWLESS moved, and it was seconded by Mr. T. ROBERTS, "That the second team captain be allowed a seat on the committee." This motion was supported by the hon. sec, and carried. PLAYERS AND THE COMAIITTEE.

Mr. I. LESSON moved " That the committee be corn- I posed of non-players, captains to be'ex-officio meMbers." In moving this he said he had no animosity to the platers, but simply desired that the best players might be selec- ted for the teams that went out. He believed there had been a little bad feeling between the players—at least he had been told so, but did not know whether it was true. (" No.") He had been told that some of the players in the first team had not even been on speaking terms with each other. (Cries of" Name.") Allow him to speak. He believed such was the ease, and he brought his mo- tion forward so that they might have independent mem- bers on the committee to choose the best players.—Mr. I T. H. Asncnorr seconded the proposal.-,Mr. J. EVANS said his experience was that the players were the most useful members of the committee. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. TINNION thought that any honours the club had to give ought to be given to the plkying members because they were the members who had brought the club to its pre- sent success. (Applause.)—On the motion being put to the meeting only two or three hands were held up for it, and it was negatived by an overwhelming majority amidst loud applause. ring SUPPLY OF GOODS, Scc. Mr. J. VANS moved "That any person who is a mem- ber of the Committee of the Warrington Football Club shall not be allowurto supply any-goods or do anywork for the aforesaid club, either directly or indirectly through any other person." He (Mr. Evans) thought that motion would commend itself. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Sairrn seconded this proposal, which, after a little dis- cussion, was agreed to. A GRATUITY.
Mr. BIBBY moved, and Mr. CRITCHLEY seconded, that the treasurer be voted a mtstity of the same amount (au> as that of last year forhis services to the club„and this was agreed to.
VOTES OF THANKS.

Mr. SMITH moved a special vote of thaliks to Mr. Win- stanley for his valuable services as auditor during the Past year.—The HON. SEC. seconded the proposition, and mentioned that they had reason to believe that Mr. Win- stanley intended leaving this country shortly. He also suggested that a testimonial ought to be presented to Mr. Winstanley, and this suggestion was warmly ap- plauded.—Mr. BRAMHALL and the PRESIDENT, supported the vote of thanks, which was carried by acclamation. A vote of thanks was also awarded the President, after which the meeting concluded.

div.head: HIL IN A THOUSAND.
div.p: HIL IN A THOUSAND.
. BY JEAN MIDDLEMASS. author of "Lady Muriers Secret," "The Spider and the Fly," "Poisoned Arrows," "Wild Georgic," &c., &c.
CHAPTER XXI. IN HIS POWER.

So rarely of late had Henry. Stanhope dined at his elnb that ho had become almost a stranger there, and not a little surprise toistified itself on the faces of more than one gossiping habitué of the place when he came into the dining-room accompanied by Prince, Sergius, who, from being a sort of lion of the season, was always looked at with interest wherever he went. The dinner had been ordered in the morning, and even such an epicure as was Prince Sergius was -,compelled to acknowledge that it was perfection and that the Heidsecker Monopole was iced to, exactly the correct degree. Considering that Henry Stanhope was by way of saving every available penny, there was little doubt that he had well studied the matter of dinners and their effect, and had come to the conclusion that the distance between a man's heart and his stomach is by no means remote. Believing this, he had nerved himself to give this entertainment thoroughly; nor did he. fail in ac- companying it by an extreme geniality of manner which was warranted in every way to put Sergius Lenskoff off his guard, and make him think that his old chum was in reality in nowise changed. Though pater-families was compelled to assume a sober tone, yet with his bachelor intimates behind the scenes, Henry Stanhope was the same good fellow he had been years ago, when sowing his wild oats in Petersburg. That it was a terrible effort for' the grate, sorely-tried man to do this, there is little doubt, and it was only on consideration of the enormity of the stake at issue, 'that he managed to keep his courage screwed to the sticking point. If Sergius Lenskoff guessed something of what was going on beneath his* old friend's 'seemingly urbane exterior, he shewed no sign of doing so, but met him with a perfectly reciprocal amount of cor- diality,- praised the 'different mets which were set before him and which in truth he seemed thoroughly to enjoy; held his glass to the light, and commented lengthily on the sparkling brilliancy of the wine, and talked gaily and brightly on subjects of general in- terest both in the present and the post-; but the long, tempting dinner had Well nigh dawdled to its close before either of the two men had .warmed into a discussion, of the matters that lay nearest both their hearts. . Good wine must, however, sobner or later have the effect of thawing the ice ; it was merely aquestion i of which disposition would succumb to its nfluence the first. Probably Sergius Lenskoff being naturally the more impetuous of the two would have tlolie so ; only from the moment he received Henry Stanhope's note in- viting him to dinner he felt sure of his game, and as long as his head kept clear from the fumes of alcohol he was determined not to spoil it by, the utterance of one•rash word.

If he had only spoken how much easier ,would Mr. Stanhope's unthawing have been ! So difficult did he find it that there is little doubt that, except under the artificial warmth produced by wine, he would not have found himself able' to thaw at, all., • - r "Tell me, Ser4ps," he said at last, quaffing a long draught of Heidseeker, and plunging :In medias VCS, "tell me of some of my old associat•.s in Petersburg. I have heard but very little of late years." '"Under existing circumstances, perhaps the less you hear the better," answered Sergius with a laugh. "How so—why so?" "Well I told you that the boy is alive." Mr. Stanhope winced. "It was a nustate, Stanhope—a terrible mistake," Lenskoff went on. "When you married Lady Fedora you should have told her." " Desidera was dead," Mr. Stanhope answered in feeble 'voice. "Aye, but the boy lived, your son, your heir." Mr. Stanhope held out his hands deprecatingly to the Prince.

—"-CII-Rad told Lady Fedora's father I hail a son he would have stopped my marriage with her at once; and you had taken the bey, and told me I should never hear of him again. I thought I had [lone enough when I impoverished my estate by raising that live thousand pounds on it for him; neither he nor anyone but you knew that he was entitled to anything. I thought I had done all that was necessar7 but God knows I have suffered much since then. • ".`Conscience makes coWards Of most men," said the Prince with a sort at sneer. The tone irritated'lVlr. Stanhope soinewhat,and he

asked, • "I wonder if you have over suffered largely for conscience sake ?" "I am no coward," answered the Prince with a half laugh, "and my shortcomings have been pecca- dilloes rather than crimes—there is but little in my past life which goes beyond the limits of that which would make most Lotharios proud; and most men are Lotharios, you know, Stanhope." "Cruelty and a gerfaral savagery of nature h which is only kept at all in subjection by the `tefinement of civilisation scarcely come within the term Lothario," answered Henry Stanhope. "Yet you are bound to recognise them as such, and to recognise in its fullest serlAe the old English proverb that "Those who live in glass houses should not throw stones."_' . "You suggested the suppression of the boy at the time of his birth; you undertook to place him out in the world on condition of my finding the necessary sum of money." "Exactly, and I fulfilled my mission both in the spirit and the letter, as an old friend should do. What fault have you to find? Your eldest son is a partner in a large furrier's in St. Petersburg, and if his business goes on increasing at its present rate, ' there is no doubt he will be able to buy up the estate of Warleigh and set the house of Stanhope on its legs again. In what have you to complain of me? And yet when I first arrived in London, after not having seen you for some years, you scarcely treated me as you were wont to do in old times." Henry Stanhope held out his hand to him. "Pardon my fears," he said, "I have suffered very cruelly of late." • Fear of what? I do not understand what you are afraid of." But Henry Stanhope did not answer ; he poured out another glass of wine and drank it. " I wonder sometimes," he went on after a short pause, "whether it would not be better to bring this young man from Russia and place him in his true position; if Geoffrey ever guesses at the truth he will do so at once." _ _ _

"Geoffrey has a noble nature, as noble as his sister's," said Prince Sergius, " but Geoffrey, if he did this thing would have the world with him, you would have it against you—better blow out your brains at once my ' poor Stanhope than try to make black white again at such a cost." "But if Geoffrey should find it out?" "He will not find it out; how can he, since no one now knows it but you 'and I, and I will tell nothing unless—" " Ah, unless what ?" "Unless I am thwarted, put ontside the pale in fact, and treated as a stranger." "You can never be treated as a stranger, Sergius, but as one of my best friends always." "'Prove it—let the family link be strengthened,and side by side let us stride over any difficulties that may present themselves in our paths. If you raked your memory you could recall several episodes in my ,1 life which are not, perhaps, wholly to my credit; but I am anxious to turn over a fresh page, and to forget them as I will forget this terrible episode of yours before you became Lady Fedora' husband, and the respectable father of a famil you now are." ' " Jam so different to you," pleaded Stanhope. " Not in the least. Otivilisation, you have just told me, refines; exactly, I acknowledge it; andlove, the love of a pure woman, humanises. Lady Fedora is a pure woman; she has known how to temper 'youi brutality of nature, and to render you—save to those who know what your past has been—the gentle courteous urbane English gentleman the world believes you to be; such being the case, why, under the softening influence of the sweet Irene, should not I cast from me the epithet of the Russian bear ? " "You really mean this; it has actually and positively entered into your mind to think of marrying my daughter?" "It has entered so thoroughly into my mind that, Irene being willing, I am determined to allow i nothing to nterfere between me and the carrying out of my intention." And thew was a fiercenessin Prince Sergius' manner as he uttered this sentence which shewed that what- , ever Irene's influence might effect in the future, for the present, at all events, he had in no wise learnt to throw off his appellation of Russian bear. " Andin the event dirty refusing my consent?" Prince Sergius did not answer for a moment, then he said, with a half smile, "You should not put a man In a difficult position by asking questions which are well-nigh impossible
o ansvi et withr at giving offence. You know yeti will—you must—consent to this marriage; of what use then to produce bad blood betweev me and inY future father-in-law ?"

Henry Stanhope winced. "Though put 111 seemingly temperate words," be answered. " this sounds very like a threat." The Prime shrugged his Shoulders. "Take it of; you like ; it matters not to me, so you give me Irene. "Fond .of money as you are, Sergius, is it no consideration to you that she will have no dot; a paltry two hundred a year wherewith to pay for her clothes, nothing more? ' "I care bothingabout her money !I want herr V Can it be that you do love my child; think of her beyond admiring her beauty, and imagine it will aq to your prestige by being attractive in Petersburg.' "I love her," said Prince Sergius, hotly, " so let us make short work of the subject." Irene's hand versus silence as to the existence of her elder brother Dathatri." "Can you not allow me a short time for reflee- tion'?" • "No. You have reflected. When you entered this Club to-night, you had thoroughly Made up your mind what yen intended to do. You know as well RS I do that the danger of an immediate revelation imminent, and you also know that your son Ferdinand's affairs are so involved that you are powerless to help him, and that the extrication or utter subversion of this young man rests entirely in my, hands. You see you fore° me to speak plainly, strenuously though I have sought to save you." Henry Stanhope held his brow in his hand, thus shielding his eyes to which the tears had risen ; his heart was too full to speak. AU that dreadful past, that weak yielding to temptation and being guilty of the sin, which, in the colonrs it had been painted , by Sergius Lenskoff, became scarcely a sin at all-- to what had it brought him now ! Even to the sacrifice of his fair young daughter. Wherever he turned she must be sacrificed ; the truth told and his dishonour proclaimed, was her ruin, while silence meant that she would become Sergius Lenskoffs wife. There was a long pause, the Prince poufing out another „brimming glass of the bright, frothY eitlseeker. "Well," he said, as, having quaffed the nectar, he set the glass once More on the table, "well, you are not wont to be irresolute when your own interests are at state." Henry Stanhope roused himself suddenly, knocking down two or three glasses in his sudden agitation. " I will give no answer whatever," he said, "but be. perfectly passive. If it please.; you to marry my darling child, settle it with her and her mother; I will neither give nor withhold mY consent. If it Pleases you to proclaim my infamy to the world and brand my sweet ,Irene's name with her father's shame, well, do your worst, I leave the issues of the past to your unravelling.' For a moment there was a gleam In Prince Sergius' eyes which boded no good ; then suddenly it changed into a bright triumph-ant light, and he stretched his hand across the table to his old friend. "Let the past be forgotten," ho said, "and have no fear for Irene with me in the future. She shall have wealth and power." Henry Stanhope did not, however, press the hand that Sergius Lenskoff tendered him ; too many dark deeds rose before his mental vision even as the Priaee was speaking for him to be able to sham any amginit; of cordiality on the subject of this vile treaty whieh was being concluded. Prince Sergius was, hoWever, satisfied. He would' perhaps have•en;;oyed more fully a decided success-- but it was enough that there was to be no opposition. Conceiving any farther discussion to be useless, he rose from the table. "What say you ?" he asked, "shall we adjourn for coffee to Your house in Eaton-square ?" , "Not to-night—my God—give me some short respite. I cannot bear any more to-night." The Prince laughed cynically. "As you like," be said, "I am your guest, so inust do your bidding." „ ' "Air—come for a saunter. I must have air, 6 pleaded Mr. Stanhope. "My poor friend, you are terribly changed. T iron constitution in which I once believed, is

generating into feminine weakness—but come; as you say, is a wholesome tonic." They passed from the dining-room into the of the club, where they met two or three men were known to both of them and each of wl looked somewhat aghast at Henry Stanhc changed appearance," sicklied o'er with the pale of thought," as it most assuredly was. On a sudden, Prince Sergius from conversing more than usually genial way with these acqin ances, left -them abruptly and made a sort of, the outer door. Peering through its glass panels were a pair of about which he could not be mistaken. They those of his confidential valet. "What is it?" he asked hurriedly. "A telegram from Russia, monsigneur I thong,h` it wise to bring it at once on the chance of find' you here ?" ' The Prince took it frcin him with a Anittered as though the coming of this piece of paper bode good, and advancing once more to the lamp in hall, he tore it open. "Nom, de Dieu,, ' he exclaimed,so loud that Stanhope, bad he been attending, must have nu.- him. And that the telegram deeply concerned Wj Stanhope there is little doubt, for the Prince look:, at him very, fixedly for a second after he had read 11! then he crushed up the paper into a ball, and thras,u, lug it into his pocket, put on the charmiug'„J persuasive manner he knew so well how to assunw and strolled up to thetnot of men. "Shall we go for our saunter. Stanhope ?'? asked.

FOREIGN NEWS.

0-14I1ERAL BOULANGER'S DISSOLUTION PROPORAT. DEFEATED. 1 _ General Boulanger has at length broken silence in the i rrench Chamber of Deputies. The Government having I declared that the time for the revision of the Constitu- I lion had not yet arrived, and that it would resign if confronted by a majority. General Boulanger has seized the opportunity, and on Monday brought forward a pro- Dosal, for which he demanded urgency, for the revision of the Constitution and the dissolution of the Chamber. Ifis speech caused a tumultuous scene. The General declared the Government to be in the hands of the privi- leged classes, and accused Ministers of drawing money from the public Treasury in order 'to secure votes from the electors. This accusation the President asked General Boulanger to withdraw, but, after merely saying that he had no intention of attacking his colleagues, the General attacked the 1 Presidency itself, asking whether a President of the ' RepUblic was really necessary, and expressing his own belief that France would get on very well without.one. After another interruption from the President, General i 7Botliang,er read his motion. Other deputies declared 'they would vote for urgency for various reasons, . although many of them repudiated all connection with The policy of the General. M. HOUSE OF' LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 20, the Rouse meeting for the first time after the Whitsuntide recess. Earl Cadogan postponed his motion as to the standing orders and tbe conduct of public business until Thurs- day. The Rochester Bishopric Bill was read a second time. The report of amendments to the Glebe Lands Bill was recaived and adopted. The Archbishop of Can- terbury postponed the third reading of the Clergy Dis- cipline Bill for a week. Their Lordships adjourned at 5 5 p.m.

THE OPERATION OVVIIE CONTAMOIT3 DISEASES ACT IN Nem—Mr. Melmime called attention to the existence and working of the Contagious Diseases Act, and of the ' Cantonment Acts in India, and moved a resolution, which would have the effect of repealing the same. He said that he and his friends demanded the ta...5..4 abolition of the Acts, and would be content with nothing less. The hon. gentleman, in a very full House, entered into the details of the working of the Act, and dwelt at length on its injustice and scandals.—Sir R. N. FOWLER seconded the opposition.—Mr. CAVENDISH BENTINCK moved an nendment to the effect that considering the large sad ,eming increase of disease in the army and navy on the home stations since the repeal of the Conta- gious Diseases Act, the House was of opinion that it was inexpedient to repeal the Acts in force in India.— Sir Joee Goner, Under-Secretary of State for India, re- plied on behalf of the Government. He did not see what more could have been done by the Government than to give a promise, as they did, diet if such practices existed RS those to which the attention of the House had been directed they should be immediately stopped, and they only hesitated when they were assnred by the Indian Government that no such practices did exist. The Acts were now suspended. (Ones of" When.") They had been suspended since the 27th March. (Hear, hear.) The Indian Government had taken this course without any pressure being placed upon it, and the Act must soon be repealed. He asked the House not to interfere with the legislative independence of the Indian Government by Forcing this matter to an issue that night —A discus- skin followed, and Sir R. TEMPLE moved an amendment to the effect that while approving 'the recent action of the Government of India, regarding the suspension of certain portions of the Contagious Diseases Act In that country, the House deemed it unconstitutional to inter- fere by resolution with that initiative in legislation which had been assigned to the Governme,nt of India by Act of Parliament. The hon. baronet, after a speech of great length, said he would refrain from moving his amendment, although he desired the House to give weight to the arguments he 'had advanced in sup- port of it.—Sir W. Foster followed, and Mr. STANSFELD then suggested that the debate should close.—On the SPEAKER putting the resolution, Mr. Biggar and some other members below the gangway challenged a division. There was evidently a very small minority, but as they persisted the SPEAKER. said, amid general 'cheers, "I will ark the clerks to come in and record the names of the minority." He then called on the Noes to stand up in their places, but no one re- sponded., and there was immediately a roar of laughter from the 'cross benches. It was evidently Mr. Biggar's intention to obtain a record of Conservatives on the subject,but the Speaker's action frustrated it, the Minis- terialista -being Willing to let the motion pass unchal- leneed rather than have to take the decisive step of vet hug. The House adjourned at 12 15 a.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

'The Speaker took the chair at a quarter after twelve o:ciodk. ILIBEL:LAW AMENDMENT BILL.—The House went into committee on the Libel Law Amendment 11111.—Mr. EzLLY,•believing it would be wrong in the interestsof ihe.public to give any further protection to newspapers, 'moved the 'omiesson of clause 2, Which proposed to repeal vection 2 of the Newspaper Libel and Registration Act, 1881. Many hon. members took part in the discussion. It was held that the bill would be invaluable to scurrilous society papers, and that it would enable pressmen to libel with ..impunity ; that it would, on the other hand, give newspaper men latitude only to de their work in a more business like way, and check the enterprise of a certain class of lawyers who did not scruple to make _gain out of spurious actions for libel. It was contended that the present law was sufficient for all purposes of, legitimate protection; and on the ,con- trary, thatmot only the reports of public meetings, but of boards e guardians and other local bodies should be ,privileged. •It was pointed out that the only proposed •change in the law was to legalise reports of meetings that are already inserted in newspapers and looked for eagerly by the public. The amendment was negatived by 181 votes against 99, and the clause agreed to and ad- ded to the bill. The clause extending privilege to re- ports of public meetings, and meetings of local bodies, including County Councils, was also agreed to. The damages °hese was under discussion at half-part five o'clock, when according to the rule, proceedings inCom- mittee were adjourned. MISCELLANaOII9.—The Victoria University Rill, after amendment, passed through Committee, and the next stage was fixed for to-morrow. The House having gone into Committee onthe Reformatory Schools Act, progress was reported, the Habitual Drunkards Act Amendment Bill passedthrough Committee, and the second -reading of the Companies Clauses Consolidation Act Amendment Bill read a second time. Mr. Jackson, replying .to Mr. Addison, said a bill relating to the law with regard to limited liability companies would be introduced in the House shortly. A hint was given to lion, members that there would be morning sittings on Tuesdays and Fri- days, wheirthe Local Government Bill was takenen those days, and the House adjourned at five minutes to six o'clock.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter after four o'clock. MISCELLAMOUS.—The Marquisof Salisbury,questioned by Lord Rosebery. was able to give little additional in- formation as to the rupture between Italy and Zanzibar. Earl Cadogan moved for a Select Committee to report on the standing orders relating to the conduct of public business. Lord Granville and Lord Salisbury spoke on the subjectrand the motion was agreed to. The Liakil- ity of Trustees Bill passed through Committee. and so did the Scoteh Universities Bill. The Premier stated that the bill for creating a Minister of Agriculture was,ready, and it was the intention of the Government to pass it this year. Their Lordships adjourned at 20 minutes pastfOght o'clock.

A CRIMINAL SHIPOWNER 'LIGHTLY PUNISHED. A hoard of Trade inquiry into the loss of the steam- hip Caerav, of Newport. with all hands. last March, was concluded at Cardiff, on Monday. The Court found that the vessel had been systemaiically overloaded on the homeward voyages,. with iron ore, from Bilbao: they also found the managing owner guilty of breach of duty, in neglecting to use reasonable means of ensuring the sea- worthiness of the vessel, by having the position of the load-line authoritatively flied; and condemned him in MO.

Hart, was charged at the Ashby-de-la-Zouch Petty Sessions, on Saturday, with an extraordinary outrage on a Cheshire gentleman, named Pierpoint. It appeared that last Lady Day Hart took a farm at Holly Hayes, about a mile from Whitchuvat, where he bad kept a beerhouse. div.head: 'LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.
div.p: THE 'LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.

/ ' THE COMPENSATION CLAUSES. A petition trom nearly 4,000 Welsh miners against the compensation clauses, will be presented to die House of Commons by Mr. Abraham. M.P. Mr. Henniker Heaton, M.P., has addressed the follow- ing important letter to the Chairman of the Conservative party in Canterbury : "House of Commons, June Ist, 1888.—My dear Capt. Lambert,—l have had an interview with the Right Hon. C. T. Ritchie, President of the Local Government Board. in reference to the numerous netitions, from all classes and sections :of the people of Canterbury, against the licensing clauses of the new Local Government Bill. On the orie hand, the licensed victuallers consid ~ • herns,elves i hardly eated in having to pay heavier lic,,sing fees, and o the other hand. the Canterbury Temperance Union, t a meeting held, I understand, under the ausreces of the Dean of Canterbury, passed resolutions against compensation of any kind, on the ground that a vested interest would be thereby acknowledged and created by the state in publican's licences. Under these circum• stances compromise is possible, and Mr. Ritchie, on be- half of the Government. has given me authority to make the following statement: 'lf a proposal is made to allo- cate the additipnal 20 per cent, license duty for the purposes of compensation, the Government will offer no ,pposition to it.' The importance of this statement will he beat understood when it is borne in mind t hat, if this amendment is carried, no further money, I understand, will be paid, or be available for compensation, and it might well be said that the con- :entious point or principle is: undisturbed, regarding the acknowledgment, or non-acknowledgment, by the state of the vested interest of the publican in his Menge. The 20 per cent, will really form an insurance fund, and will not be contributed by the public. I shall be glad if you will publish this letter, so that public opinion tnay be elicited on the proposal.—Very faithfully yours, I. liessittra HEATON."

It is stated that several of the supporters of Mr. Glad- stone. and also a considerable section of the Irish party, intend to support the principle of compensation to pub- licans whose licenses are withdrawn without any breach of the conditions on which they were granted. A meeting of Liberal,Unionist leaders was held in one of the committee-rooms of the House of Commons, on Monday, to discuss the compensation clauses of the Local Government Bill and other matters. Lord Hartington iiresided. and amongst those present were Mr. Chamber- lain. Sir Henry Junes, Lord Edward Cavendish, and Mr. Craig Sellar. The proceedings were of a conversational ,haracter. It is believed that those present agreed as to !he desirability of supporting the Government on the ticensine question, it being intimated to the meeting that some modification of the compensation clauses in the direction of a time limit was in contemplation. The ,!onsultation lasted nearly an hour.

div.head: ROWDYISM AT BIRMINGHAM.
div.p: ROWDYISM AT BIRMINGHAM.

A demonstration against the licensing clauses of tho Local Government Bilk especially those relating to the e.lmpensation of publicans deprived of their licenses, was attempted in Birmingham Town Hall on Monday fhe'promoters furnished their friends with tickets, giving them favourable opportunity of entrance to the hall, but '!r ups of people organised by the public-house party got possession of fully two-thirds of the building, and raised a clamour, which prevented a solitary speaker from being heard beyond the reporters. The Earl of Lichfield presided, and Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P., and Alderman Powell Williams, M.P., were to have spoken. Mr. Caine. speaking tO the reporters. claimed :iberty for Liberal Unionists to vote against the Govern- tnent upon this question. The question of the union of the kingdom and the empire was absolutely, safe for the period of the present Parliament, unless the Govern- ment chose deliberately to endanger It. If the clauses were passed he should give notice of a bill"to repeal ;hem, and raise such a temperance crusade in the country that no Government cquld stand it. The only resolution passed was one for the adjournment of the meeting, which was lost by a large majority, but de- clared carried. . THE TOWN-COUNTY QUESTION.

Mr. Leake. M.P., writing to the Clerk of the Farnworth Local Board relative to the Local Government Bill, say, there will be a considerable extension of the principle whereby boroughs will be made counties, and that the scheme will include certain ancient and county towns with a less population than 50,000. finless some alleviation were proposed, this extension would make the hard MSC the Local Board of Farnworth had set forth all the •arder ; but he had no doubt this alleviation would .Je found in some proposal to place the cost of mainten- ance and repair of main roads entirely on the funds which were to be forwarded in aid of local rates. In this rase, inasmuch as these funds were derivable in great part from the populous places which were to be made counties, the unfair burden would be removed from ths more sparsely populated urban and rural districts within slich counties as Lancashire.

div.head: ANTI-COMPENSATION DEMONSTRATION IN HYDE PARK.
div.p: ANTI-COMPENSATION DEMONSTRA- TION IN HYDE PARK.

On Saturday afternoon agreat demonstration was held in Hyde Park, London, against the compensation clauses in the Local Government Bill. According to the arrange- ments of the promoters-in the procession, which marched from the Embankment, were included members of the tiritish Women's Temperance Associations, Bands of Hope Unions, and the Liberal and Radical Clubs of various districts in the metropolis. The meeting was not fully constituted until half-past six. There wore numerous bands and banners in the assembled crowd, and ten platforms were prepared with vehicles. Lord Kinnaird presided at the: first. and Professor Stuart, M.P., Mr. William Johnston, M.P., and Sir W. Law,!ott, M.P., Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P., and others were chairmen at the remaining ones. The proceedings con- tinued until half-past seven, speeches being delivered by the chairmen mentioned and other members of Parlia- ment, and by Mrs, Atherton, Mrs.t Lynn, and several other ladies, Resolutinas were carried emphatically pro- testing against the proposal to create a vested interest In drink as unjust to ratepayers and tending to encour- age intemperance and its attendant evils. Sir WILFRID LAWSON said the large gathering reminded him somewhat of a contested eleetien—Southampton, for example. (Cheers, and cries of "No politim.") He congratulated his friends upon the enormous gathering'. But honour should be given to whom it was due. It was sa rnat he was restionsible• for the demonstration, but that was net the care, for the initiative and subsequent organisation had been carried out by the aid and pecu- niary assistance of Mr. Charrington. What, had they met for' To turn out the Tories? No.„ But they had met to compel them to do right. Their motto was that of the volunteers, "Defence, not defiance." They had met to defend themselves from the great liquor ring which had been alarwed to rule this country too long. Fer many generations past they had taken the people's money for selling drink, and now they 'wanted to take their money for not selling drink, (Laughter.) The licensing proposals before the House of COmtrions Were the most extraordinary and revolting that had ever been laid before an assembly in a free nation, and if the people of England did not resist them successfully he should begin to think that the manliness of the people of this country hal departed from them. They must, not think that this battle was going to he won lightly, nor that there was no danger ; for in reality the battle was a tough one anti-the danger was great. (Hear, hear.) What WAS the danger? It. Nina the drink, The Govern- ment of the day depended for its support upon the hrewera and publicans, and the bargain between them n as, that if the Government gave them a vested interest in what Mr. Gladstone had called an estate the nublicans would do their best to keep the Government in power; but, the liquor ring, if they did not get their price out of the money of the country, would kick the Government out at the first opportunity. (Cheers.) If the publicans had to pay conlpensad ion themselves thev. would endeavour to get it out of somebody, and they would do it by increasing the sale of drink, 'and that would by no means please the temperance party. (Hear, hear.) They were really trying to help the Tories, for they were now bolid slaves to the brewers and publicans. Instead of trying to turn the Government o•d, they wete doing all they could to emancipate them from the slavery under which they were labouring. (0 eers.) This was no party fight. It was a national struggle against a greaf veste4l interest. That it was not a partt., matter Was proved by' the fact that a good sound Tory in Parliament had proposed to do away with the licensing clauses. There were some Liberal 'Unionists Wll,i would do the same. That they had the nation with them was shown not so much by the immense assemblage in the park that day as by the Southampton election. (Hear, hear.) This was one of the greatest crises The temperance party had ever encountered, and Hwy had arrayed against them the powers of evil and of darknms. But they had truth and justice on their side, if not the great and mighty and wealthy; and truth and justice were yet dear to the hearts of the people of Eng- land. (Cheers.) Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P., who presided at one of the plat- forms, delivered a speech in.which he strongly denounced the compensation clauses. Amid much cheering herald-. that rather than see the clauses passed as they stood at present he would seethe Government defeated.
There was no disturbance in the park or on the ro,:l 4. to and frorn'tke meeting.

STA RTIANC3 DISCOVERY' IN WODCESTERSITIRE.—T4IB Worcesterskire police have a sensational case in hand in the northern part of the county. • The body of a boy, of apparently four to five years, who has unquestionably been murdered, has been found in a well near Shatter- ford, on the boundary of .the county. The inquest was opened on Monday, and adjourned. The premises where the body was found have horn dosed two years, and the well must have been opened with difficulty to put the body in.—The Worcestershire police, on Tuesday, arrested a labourer, name Wyre, on a charge of murdering his son, five years of age, at Wolverlev, near Kidderminster. The man separated from his wife some months ago, and n Monday took the boy away with him. The child's body was found at the bottom of a well, and the police have obtained evidence which they believe will clearly establish the criminality of the father.
