Mr. Gladstone teed both lessons at the Hawarden Church on Sunday morning, and in the afternoon walked through the village with Mr. Fierbert Gladstone. A great Unionist demonstration will be held at the Marquis of Abergavenny's seat, Eridge Park, near Maid- stone, on July 18th. Mr. Balfour will 1373 the chief peaker. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone left Hawarden for London. on Monday, driving through the village from the Rectory to the Castle, and then to Sandvcroff, whence train wai taken to Chester, and the 11 30 train to Euston was caught there.

_ A Cabinet Council—the first since the Whitsuntide recess—was held at the Foreign Office, on Mbnday, all the Ministers being present. The meeting broke up shortly after 2 30, having discussed the compensation clauses of the Local Government Bill.

The Hawick Unionist Association hive adopted the recommendation of the recent meeting of the representa- tives from Flawick, Galashiels, and Selkirk, to select Mr. Austen Chamberlain, son of the Right Bon Joseph Chamberlain, as the candidate for the Bowler Burghs. The St. James's Gazette, of Monday, says :—The French Government are publishing, for the use of the naval commanders, a minutely detailed description of the for- tifications and armaments of all British possessions, together with the Imperial and, local forces available for their defence. Charts and plans are attached. The members interested in women's suffrage met on Monday and agreed to present a memorial to Mr. W. II smith, asking that facilities should be given for Baron Dimsdale's bill for the enfranchisement of women bouFe- holders. A resolution was also passed expressing satis- faction at the recognition of the principle of women's suffrage in the Local Government (Electors) Bill.

Mr. Gladstone. acknowledging a copy of a resolutior passed by the Bury Liberal Association, condemning the votes given by Sir Henry James, the borough member, writes as follows :—" Undoubtedly the Dissentient Liberals have given the policy of the present Govern- ment, and that not on Ireland exclusively, a support much more effective than could have been given by the same number of Tories. There is hardly any single person whose participation in this course I more pro- foundly regret than Sir Henry James."

div.head: AYR BURGHS CONTEST.
div.p: THE AYR BURGHS CONTEST.

Mr. Evelyn Ashley addressed a meeting of the -Liberal Unionist supporters at Ayr on Saturday. He said he had been chosen to contest the seat because he had contested Bridgeton, the result of which had been a foregone con- clusion, though it was considered important to challenge Sir George Trevelvan's rapid political apostacy. The Southampton election was not •lost on Home Rule or the compensation clauses, but because the electors thought an unfair advantage had been taken of the absence ol the Gladstonian csndidate.— A meeting of Rome Rulers, held in the Catholic Schools, the parish priest in the chair, decided to support Mr. Sinclair. The writ was received at Avr on Tuesday morning, and the returning officer fixed the nomination for Satur• day next, and the polling for the following Friday. Several representatives of the labour party, including Mr. Threlfall, Southport; Mr. Uttley. Sheffield; and Mr. Champion, London, have gone to Ayrshire to place their views before the Liberal candidate, and before the elec- tion will confer with the Radical representatives at Westminster.
LORD HARTINGTON ON LIBERAL DIFFERENC ES

The annual dinner of the members of the Palmerston Club, in the University of Oxford, took place on Satur- day evening, in the Town Hall, the chair being taken by the president, Mr. G. G. A. Murray (St. John's College). Ttiere was a lirge company, among whom were the Mar- quis of Hartingten, Lord Herschell. Lord Lymington, the Warden of Merton, Mr. H. H. Fowler, M.P., Mr. O. Russeil, the President of Magdalen, Mr. W. R. W. Peel. and Mr. Orange.—The PRESIDENT gave the toast of the Liberal party. Lord Ilenvistcyrox, in responding, said he entered public life under Cord Palmerston, and his name wa, associated to him with unswerving honesty and fixity of purpose. It was customary on thewq occa- sions to paint glowing pictures of the present and the future; but if there was any truth in the saying tat rimo veritas he should have expected that after dinner speakers would have more than usual frankness in re- cognising unpleasant facts. He thought no good came from dissembling as to their differences. He deplored the condition of the Liberal party, which made it impos- sible for it to carry on the work which had seemed to be before it in 1885. He was not greatly moved by the failure of the Liberal party to abolish the death duties and to deal with the licensing question, sines, unlike Mr. Gladstone, he considered these questions as mat- ters of minor importance, certain to be settled soon, and which, therefore, should not interfere with the consideration of a question vitally affecting the Constitution. He recognised the importance of the Irish question as much as any of the previous speakers, and regretted that the Liberal party were not able to apply their former principles and former methods to continue their work in Ireland, carried on from 1869 to 1884. The proposal of Home Rule he regarded as a de- claration that the Liberal party was incompetent to deal with Ireland on Liberal principles, as he hunself thougt,t that the Imperial Parliament was fully able to deal with every part of the United Kingdom. Therefore, he honestly desired that it should be possible for the Liberal party again to unite, and to deal in its former manner with Irish as in otliAr., matters. Until a recent date the work of the Liberal party had been destructive and rightly so, for there was much that was bad and re- quired change; but now there was a svork of construc- tion before it in meeting the growing s7cial needs of the time. The days ot obstructive Toryism were over, and without, revard to names he should continue to support those who in his opinion were meeting this question of Home Rule in the best manner. On this question of supreme importance he was divided„from the Majority of the Liberal tarty, and So long aVtliev advocated a course which, in his opinion, was most perilous to tile interest of the country,. he would be compelled to sup- port those with whom he was in agreement OD this vital qiiestiOn. (Loud cheers.) .

MR. SETONSARR, M.P., AT ST. HELENS.

Mr. Henry Seton-Karr, M.P., for the borough, ar-- rived in St. Helens on Monday, on returning from his Whitsuntide holidays in Scotland. In the after- noon and evening he visited the rooms of the Con- servative Club in Hall-st., where a good many mem- bers had assembled to meet him. Mr. Seton-Karr first received a deputation of insurance agents, consisting of Messrs. May, Humphries, Penning- ton (Royal Liver Friendly Society), Coulter, Bolton (Vic- toria Friendly), Sowerbutts, Baxter, Cox Tither, Hughert (Prudential), and Waterworth. Forbes, Miller, and Phillips (Wesleyan and General.) The deputation expressed to the hon. member their grievances, and asked if he would watch their interests in any measure that might be introduced bearing on the management of such societies. Mr. Seton-Karr said he had not had the privilege of seeing Sir John Lubbock's Friendly Societies Bill, which had been alluded to. He understood their chief grievances were that reductions were being made in the rates of percentage on the money they col- lected, and that they were not fairly treated in the way of compensation. He would make a point of watching the measure, and he hoped they would send him a copy of the amendments they wished moving, and if he could see his way to move them, he would do so. The hon. gentleman next received a deputation from the" St. Helens Jurymen's Association," who complained of the unfairness of tradesmen and others being re- peatedly called upon coroner's juries and to go to Liver- pool to the sessions without any compensation. They thought a clause might be inserted in the Local Govern- ment Bill, authorising jurymen to be remunerated from the rates.—Mr. Seton-Karr said he thought the effect of the Local Government Bill, if anything, would be that of increa.sing the rates, and everyone of such proposals meant an additional burden upon the rates; and there- fore it was a matter forserious consideration how far they were going to throw on rates. He would k consider the matter, and do what he could. . _ _

In the evening Mr. Seton-Karr addressed a good num- ber of the members and friends who gathered in the bil- liard-room of the club. In the course of his remarks he said that during the last three or four ifiontlis they had been doing a good deal of work in Parliament. They were doing work which he thought must be very inter- esting to all working men and ratepayers, and, in fact, all classes in the kingdom. They had got the Local Government Bill on the stocks, an this week they were going into committee on it. The present Government had been pretty considerably abused by their opponents during the past year. They were abused because they en- forced the law in Ireland ,which their opponents said was coercion, and they were abused for bringing in the Local Government Bill, which their opponents said was a Drink Bill; and so they said the Government was not only one of coercion, but also one of drink. It seemed to him that if there was one thing they might congratu- late themselves on, it was that the Government had brought in a thnrougly sound liberal measure, and a • measure which reflected every possible credit on the man who had drawn it up, and by the time it had passed, as no doubt it would pass, it would be the crowning evi- dence of the work of the session. Personally, he (Mr. Seton-l Carr) thought he was rather in favour of the drink clauses, if they would like his opinion; but he referred to the measure because it showed that the policy of the present Government were based on sound princi- ples, which would bear the test of time and experience. It showed a desire to place power in the hands of the people—a desire to see people in the counties, as well as in the boroughs, manage all questions affecting them- selves more on their own responsibility, and less from the central authority of Parliament.—On the call of Mr. B. Biram, LP., three hearty cheers were givor for Mr. Seton-Karr.

Son's ironmongery- warehouse, Stephen's-green, Dublin, and Mr. Booth's watch factory, adjoining, were destroyed by fire on Thursday morning. The loss is considerable. A Limerick landlord named Cahill is reported to have been fired at from behind a hedge and shot in the head and neck. A coroner's jury on Thursday evenimr returned a verdict of murder against Wyres, the man who is charged with the murder of his little son by throwing him into a well. The coroner described the crime a 8 black and inhuman.

SHOCKING sTRAGEDY IN SCOTLAND—On Thursday, a shocking tragedy took place at Coupar Angus. A short time ago a Mrs. Don, wife of a slater, obtained a judicial separation from her husband. This preyed on the man's mind, and on Thursday morning he went to a neighbour— ing farm, where his wife was employed, and fired a pistol at her. She fell backwards, ,slightly wounded in the bead, but her husband, supposing he had killed her, in- stantly shot himself dead.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 9, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 9, 1888.

question of the" proposed compensation to brewers and publicans under the Local Govern- Ment Bill is exciting deep interest throughout the e°ontry, and for the time it overshadows even the agitation for Home Rule for Ireland. Not that , sentient Liberals lose sight of Home Rule; their opposition to it is a matter with them of Life or death, politically speaking; and we need tot be surprised, therefore, to hear the rumour that they decided, at a meeting held on Monday, with Lord HARTINoToN in the chair, to take into favour- able consideration the action of the present Government in giving compensation to brewers, ' rather than, as Mr. GLADSTONE puts it, run the risk ri bringing in a Government that would give %me Rule to Ireland. Their degradation is, therefore, complete. There was a time when 111,tey might assume to control the policy of the 11.°1•Y party; but it has come to be realised that ! ffissentient Liberals are of little or no account 4t a contested election; and the Tories can " afford to say that HARTINGTON AND COM- PA ir must be content for the future to keep their noses to the Tory grindstone. Then there is the Southamoton election, which has opened the I.eyes of the Ministry to the fact that Liberal `Joionism is nothing—whilst compensation is every- Sc‘the screw has been applied ; the "issentients are to support the Tories on the ques- tion of compensation, or there will be a dissolution, . hich means that they would go under and be '4°on no more. How things are changed since Lord .k.LISBURY had to frighten his followers by telling them there would be a dissolution if they did not Yield to the Dissentients in the matter of the re- vision of Irish judicial rents! 0, this dissolution --what a terror it is to parliamentary evil-doers! tut, stave it off as long as they can, it will come; and then how will they stand after having for so long deceived and defrauded the electors? This is a question which is causing searching of heart amongst the members of the mongrel party which is for the moment in a majority in the House of Commons. There are Liberal Unionists who have already. slipped further down the inclined plane than is agreeable to them; and there are some, like Mr. CAINE, who draw the lino at compensa- tion to "the trade," and say—" We will have none Of it." But let the public take heed there is a real danger that the compensation clauses will be Passed, in one bad form or another, notwithstand- ing such a magnificent demonstration as that in London, on Saturday, and others which are being held throngliont the country. The present House has had no mandate on this question, and there is reason to believe that it is a long way behind the rest of the nation. It is significant that there has been no serious attempt, either on the part of the Liberal nionists or of the Tories, to defend the compensa- tion clauses 'as they stand in the bill; but a more et less skilful effort has been made to minimise their importance. Mr. RITCHIE, in particular, has °°,ught to make it out, after the fashion of "Mr. lOots," that they are of "no consequence." But the electors are alive V) the issue, and they are !lot to be led astray by smooth, misleading words. -1-110 fact is the Government ,have shamefully hnngled in the matter; they were entirely wrong to begin with, in their view of the law; and now that the Court of Queen's Bench has decided ] against their contention, they haven't the honesty t? admit that they are in the wrong. Theques- tion, as it seems to us, is a very simple one: either ~ . license-holder has, or has not, a legal estate in his license extending beyond the twelve months for which it is granted. If he has, it must be frankly acknowledged; and, if the license is can- celled, he must be paid. If, on the other hand, it be found that the law does not recognise, and 11ever has recognised, such an estate, he must be told that compensation is altogether out of the l'lllestion. He must be required to obey the law as it is decided in the highest courts of the land, as to people are required t. obey it. With regard r compromise, of which we hear so much, it is not 1.0 be thought of where the question of principle, is involved As "the trade" has mnde.its bed so let it Ile, Heaven only knows how terrible are some io_f,the beds of its making in which other people aro o•Ynmg ; and if there is to be a new claim set up c)ne side, a new claim, will be set up on the Other. Let electors be careful, therefore, how they Commit themselves even to such a proposal as that aleh Sir WILLIAM ROLDSWORTH, M.P., makes on

-------- behalf of the Church of England Temperance Society. The amendment of which he has given notice is that compensation shall be assessed on thebasis of the difference (if any) between the "gross annual rental of the licensed premises as- certained for the purpose of levying the poor-rate immediately before the passing of this Act and the an- nual letting value of such premises after the license has been deter mined the arbitrator being empowered to award a sum not exceeding ten times such dif- ference." This means that if a public-house now rented at £lOO should, after the loss of its license, be deemed to be worth f.:50 a year only for other purposes, the compensation shall not exceed £5OO, that sum being ten times the difference between the old rent and the now rent. But why grant anything? Not a penny has been granted to the hundreds of licensed victuallers who have failed to obtain a renewal of licenses in the past; and we hold that not a penny should be paid for the future. From 1875 to 1885 something like 1,000 licenses were refused; but no. compensation was granted; and why, in the name of fair play to the taxpayers and to the late holders of these licenses, should compensation be granted in case 1,000 o r 10,000 licenses are refused during the next ten years? But apart from this fundamental objec- tion, we foresee that Sir WILLIAM HOLSDWORTH'S proposal would work inequitably. He has some- thing to learn if he does not know that the rental, even as determined by reference to the rate book, has little or no relation, in many cases, to the busi- ness done, or to the value of a house as a licensed house. Those who are in the swim will tell him that there are hundreds of beersellers and publicans who do not, in reality, pay rent at all. They are tied to the brewer to sell a minimum quantity, which is taken as covering the rent. The brewer is, in nine cases out of • ten, the all-important factor; and it is not too much to say that, if Englishmen are such fools as to tax themselves in this matter, .900 out of every £l,OOO that is paid for compensation will go to men who have grown enormously rich through the degradation of their fellow-men. Compensation to publicans, except at the hands of the brewers who have fattened on the monopolies which they have so long enjoyed, would be a folly and a crime, and as such should be resisted to the uttermost by the electors, and irrespective of sect, creed, or party.

Warrington Town Councillors were usefully ern- , I ployed on Tuesday vening in discussing, at some length, the various matters of importance which came before them. It is too much the practice to take it for granted that the recommendation of each committee must be accepted as the best that can be done under the particular circumstances. No doubt a particular committee is the best judge, as a rule, of what it is advisable to do; but it sometimes happens that the members are found thinking more of the department in which they aro interested than of the Corporation as a whole. Besides, however sound the judgment of a Com- mittee may be, there is nothing lost by demonstra- ting its soundness in the course of free discussion. The ratepayers are somebody, after all, and they are entitled to know something—not only as to what thing's are being done, but as to why they are being done. The first point of interest, on Tuesday, arose out of the request of Dr. GORNALL, the Medical Officer of Health, to bo permitted " to exercise a small amount of practice," with the assurance on his part that he would not let it in any way interfere with his duties as a public officer. The Sanitary Committee recommended that the ' request be acceded to, a recommendation which was ultimately adopted by fourteen votes to nine, in opposition to an amendment proposed by Coun- cillor PLATT with the object of referring the request back "for further consideration, either to define exactly its terms, or otherwise, as the committee might think desirable." Speaking of the matter in the abstract, it is no doubt advisable for Cor- porations to refrain from giving their officials permission for private practice ; but, as the particular case s t pod, the Medical Officer of Health felt, after over ten years of service conscientiously discharged, that he was entitled to ask for a privilege of this kind, or that an advance of salary should be given him. Having regard to the fact that, as Alderman Bun_ GESS put it, Dr. GORNALL is "not keeping pace with the day in his profession," and to the equally important consideration that every advance of salary is a further burden upon the ratepayers, we cannot but think that the Medical Officer of Health has done the right thing in the course he has taken. Councillor PLATT contended that the Medical Offi- cer of a borough which had nearly 50,000 inhabi- tants ought to devote the whole of his time to the duties. We are not inclined to minimise the im- portance of these duties; but it is due to those who have supported the recommendation of the Sanitary Committee to state that it is usual to al- low private practice to Medical Officers of towns larger even than Warrington. There is Wigan, for instance, with a population of over 50,000, St. Helens with 60,000, Stockport with over 60,000, and Blackburn with 120,000. At each of these towns, private practice is allowed to the Medical Officer of Health.

With the retirement of Mr. JAMES PATERSON from the management of the Corporation Gas ' Works, the Gas Committee have wisely taken ad- vantage of the opportunity thus afforded them to reorganise the staff; and there .can be scarcely any question that they have done well in proposing to separate the purely secretarial work from the gas manager's department. The change involves, as Councillor HENRY ROBERTS argued, an entire re- construction of the management of the Gas Works; and it is due alike to the Town Council as a whole, and to the ratepayers gener- ally, that an' important matter of this kind should be well considered before a final decision is taken. Alderman HOLMES, as chairman of the Committee, offered no objection, it should he stated, to the matter being adjourned until the next meeting of the Council. The re- commendation of theGasCommittee,which is most questoped, and most questionable, is that Mr. PATERSON should, notwithstanding his retirement, havearetainingfee of £lOO a year "for the purpose of consultation and advice, so long as it might be ad‘sable that the arrangement be continued." On the face of it we should say that the proposed arrangement is a bad one; and, unless there is some reason for it which has not yet been given, it ought not to be adopted. If Mr. HADDOCK, who is to be the new manager, cannot be trusted to do the work of a manager without being put in leading strings in this way, the pub- lic ought to be told that ho is still in training, and he should be content with something less than :e3OO a year. If, howevor, the committee can speak of him as fully competent in their judgment for the post, ho should be allowed to accept it with a free hand. It may be that Mr. HADDOCK, as a younger man than ME. PATERSON, will have methods of his , own in management. If he is worth his salt, he ; will have some capacity for initiation, and I should be allowed to take his own course without

having to consider whether it would be likely to secure the approval of the late manager: £lOO a year is altogether too much to pay for advice which may not, after all, be needed. It would be far better, as it seems to us, to free Mr. PATERSON entirely from responsibility, and allow him to en- joy in peace his well-earned rest. He can, of course, be consulted when it is found necessary, just as a lawyer or docter is consulted—when it is found necessary. But, above all, let the new manager have, as the Americans say, " a fah show."

YESTERDAY afternoon, in the House of Com- mons, Sir HENRY JAMES brought forward his. amendnient to the Local Government Bill, the ob- ject of which is to constitute every borough that at present contains 50,000 inhabitants a county by itself. Mr. Ruciun, on behalf of the Government, accepted the amendment; and said there were a few other boroughs under 50,000 which they would admit to the privilege of being counties—if the botoughs themselves desired it. Those were :—Exoter, Worcester, Chester, Lincoln, Gloucester, and Canterbury. It will be observed that the places named as having this special privilege thrown at them—for the Government do not wait till they are asked—are all cathe- dral cities. But why draw. the line at pla.es that are already privileged .in that they are cities? Is it on the principle of giving to him that already hath much? It will be a standing discredit to the Government, if Warrington and other similar boroughs are excluded, after granting the concession to still smaller boroughs. With the exception of Exeter, not one of the favoured cities had a population, at the census of 1881, as largo as that of Warrington. The figures areas follows, tak- ing the population in each case for the last census, and for the parliamentary borough, which is generally somewhat larger than the municipal borough :
- I—Exeter 47,098 4—Lincoln 37,312 2—Worcester ...... 40,421 s—Gloucester 36,552 3—Chester. 40,342 6—Canterbury 21,701

- - - . Warrington 45,253. It is hardly necessary to say that Warrington, since the census of 1881, has grown more rapidly than. the majority of these places; so that on the score of population it is ahead of all but Exeter, if not of Exeter itself. It is to be hoped that a special meeting of the Town Council, if not of the inhabitants, will be immediately called, and that active measures will be taken to bring it home to the Government that, in view of the concession made, a great wrong will be done if Warrington is not also scheduled amongst the boroughs that are to become counties.

The Newton Commissioners are like the old womap who had so many children that she didn't know what to do. They were offered a plot of land for a Recreation Ground as a jubilee gift from Mr. Legh and Mr. T. W. Legh; but as they made no sign, they have now the alternative offer of land in Williamson-square, with a subscrip- tion of £5OO, towards a Public Hall. The Com- missioners seem to think that in either case they Will have a white elephant on their hands; but, as they don't know what to do, had they not better call a Town's Meeting, and let the ratepayers' , decide?

The special meeting, in Manchester, on Mon- day, to promote the new bill in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal undertaking, passed off very satisfactorily. Mr. T. A. Walker, the con- tractor for the works, was present, and, at the call of the shareholders, gave some aceoant of the pro- gress that is being made. Mr. Walker is not like Byron; he is not elated to findthat ho "awoke up one morning and found himself famous." Ile is a quiet, hard-working man : but lie can do his work: and there is no reason to doubt that, at the end of four years froni the commencement of his con- , tract, the Ship Canal will be an accomplished feat.

Mr. Seton-Karr, M.P., had cold comfort for the representatives of the " St. Helens Jurymen's Association," who pleadtta that jurymen should be remunerated from the rates. He said it was a matter for "serious consideration" whether they should throw such a burden on the rates. He was dreadfully glum at the prospect of a fow thousands passing into the hands of tradesmen in payment for services rendered; but he was quite cheerful, later on, at the idea of payinginillions out of the rates to brewers who have no title to a penny. We do not say this is inconsistent; all we say is that it is Toryism of the Seton-Karr type, and should be rejected at St. Helens.

They have a way of their own of showing their friendship at the Earlestown Conservative Club. There seems to have been what ordinary people would call a serious row at the club, which resul- ted in two men being charged with maliciously wounding a member named Thomas Pill. One of the men has gone to America, and left.no address ; and the other, Joseph Wrigley, was brought up at the County Sessions on Wednesday. Mr. Richard- son, solicitor, of Bolton, pleaded that Pill and Wrigley should be allowed to retire and see if they could" cement their friendship." They were per- mitted to do so; and now people are wondering in Earlestown if the cement will stick, and whether the cement is of such a patent kind that it can only be used in police courts as between members of Conservative clubs.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
The Americans have invented a new term for the "dude," otherwise known as " masher." The new word has just the right feminine touch—it is "sissy."
Mr. Jay Gould, according to Mr. Jay Gould's son, is not ill; but that does not mean, of course, that Mr. Jay Gould is not "an ill un."

The State of New York has just passed a bill to substitute death by electricity for hanging. This is so great an improvement upon the old method that it may truly be described as" capital" punish- ment.

The London correspondent of the "Dublin Ex- press" says that the King-Harman Bill will be dropped. This much is certain, that the Govern- ment are not pressing it forward; it is dropped for the present. They find that Colonel King-Harman is a too hot potatoe.

Tho latest record of the time from Queenstown to New York is six days, one hour, and fifty-five minutes. This feat was accomplished by the Cunard steamship, Etruria, which reached Sandy Hook on Saturday last. If this sort of thing goes on, we shall be having excursions to Niagara--there and back in ten days.

The dealers in war scares have succeeded again. This time, as the result of the thumping of the military drum, the nation has had 1;2,600,000 squeezed out of it. This—an, addition to the usual thirty millions—is about eighteen pence per head for every .man, woman, and child in the United Kingdom. It is an impudent robbery.

Jackson, the Manchester murderer, seems to be here, there, and everywhere—except where he should be, in gaol. The "active and intelligent officer" has made a large number of "clever captures ;" i so many that he s tempted to play pranks with Shakespeare and exclaim : I think there be six Jacksons in the field— Five have I lagged to-day instead of him.

Mr. Goschen has had to "climb down" in the matter of the wine duties; it seems that he has been misinformed. He has been misinformed, too, as to the operation of the wheel tax; and if he will only climb down as much in this matter, too, he will be regarded as almost as great an adept in the fine art of stultification as the Prime Minister him- self.

The fact that largo numbers are at- tracted to Warrington Park "when the band begins to play" evinces a genuine fondness for music among the masses. People certainly do not attend to see mid hear the "fellow- lads," who should be compelled to "move on" and away, if they cannot behave themselves. Couldn't Mr. Hunt spare an extra constable, whose sole duty it should be to "walk into 'em"?

The "Morning Post" says :—"The bill promised by the Marquis of Salisbnry with respect to the creation of life peers will be presented next week." According to Lord Stanley of Alderley, new life peers would be so much " rubbish " added to the House of Lords. But what does it matter? We shall deal with the whole rubbish heap in "the sweet by-and-by."

The latest rumour as to the compensation clauses is that the Government will fight them up to the division lobby, and if defeated go on with- out them. This would certainly be after the man- nor of Lord Salisbury. How convenient when people are not hampered with principles--when they can be thrown overboard to save an other- wise sinking ship! "But a time win come" &c., "as the man in the play says."

James Hayes, of Widnes, aged 14, is a cool thief. While a pawnbroker's assistant was out of the shop, he entered, took a bundle containing a suit of clothes, snatched off the ticket, and on the assistant returning offered the property in pledge, and received 12s from the unwary shopman. We shall hear more of this lad. Give him the chance, and he will run a hard race with Jay Gould.

The Rev. S. Rogers, vicar of St. Mark's, Liver- pool, has been brought before the Consistory Court for holding an Orange Lodge, and keeping its regalia, in church. It seems that thero were also three candlesticks; but Mr. Rogers urged that they were "very little ones." . There was a young woman once who came with a baby mal a propoß ; and when reproached with the matter she, too, pleaded that it was a "very little one." There is nothing new, it seems, under the sun.

It is suggestive of the way in which the Govern- ment have made a mess of it, that both candidates in the Ayr Burghs contest aro opposed to the com- pensation clauses. The fight is, therefore, on the Homo Rule question pure and simple. The Hon. Evelyn Ashley is tho Liberal-Unionist-and-Tory candidate, while Mr. James Sinclair upholds the Liberal flag. It is a daring, if not a hopeful,

ACCIDENT AT WlDlsTEß.—Whilst following his employ- ment at the works of Messrs. Hall Brothers and Shaw, West Bank, William Griffiths. of 29, Bridge-st., acciden- tally fell into a liquor vat, and seriously scalded his foot. Under the care of Dr. Hutchinson he is progressing favourably. VICTORIA-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL. WIDNES.—The an- niversary services were held on Sunday, when the Rev. W. Humphreys, of Bradford, preached morning and evening to good congregations. In the afternoon the Rev. E. Hall, of the United Methodist Free Church, Run- corn, delivered RR address to the scholars. The collec- tions realised a total sum of £Bol7s 4d. "Ts GREATEST CHARACTER IN Ilisrony."—This was the title of a lecture delivered in Victoria-road Chapel, Widnes, on Wednesday evening, by Mr. Downes, of Lon- don, editor of "Great Thoughts." Mr. H. Wade Deacon occupied the chair, and there was a capital attendance. The lecture was a powerful description of the life of Christ. A collection was taken in aid of the renovation fund. RUNCORN STARI2-IIOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY (NO. 2).— In `connection with this society a branch office was opened at Frocittham on Wednesday evening„ when a pub- lic meeting was held in Booth's Assembly-room. There was a fair attBnda nee, and Mr. S. Pope, of. Runcorn, Oc- cupied the chair. Mr. W. Handley, the secretary, ex- pained The principle upon which the ballot for appro- priation was made, and Thomas Lloyd, signalman, of Ellesmere Port, was entitled to £2OO, free of interest, for 14 years. WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—The third annual meet- ing of the executive council of the Widnes Division Liberal Association was held in the Reform Club, Dale-st., Liverpool, on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. E. Carey oc- cupied the chair. There was a: large attendance of re- presentatives from different parts of the division. After a vote of thanks to the retiring officers, Mr. B. K. Mus- pratt was unanimously re-elected president, and Mr. W. B. Bowring treasurer. The remaining business was of a private character. WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.—ThO monthly, meeting was held at the Town Hall yesterday. Mr H. Wade Deacon presiding. The Librarian reported that the total attendance in the reading room for the past month had been 11,950, being an average of 470 per day forthe2B days the Library had been open, and was an increase of 2,541 as compared with the corresponding month of last year. The committee determined to spend about £7O in purchasing new books. As the old catalogue is sold out, the committee considered the advisability of printing a new edition. It was decided to make an application to the Gilchrist Education Trust for a course of lectures at Widnes. The Chairman under- undertook, with the nnanimous sanction of the commit- tee, to act as local secretary. A SMART YOUNG THIEF AT WIDNES.--Jannes Hayes, 14 years of age, was brought before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday, charged with stealing a suit of clothes, value 255, from the shop of Horatio Syred, pawnbroker, Waterloo-road. During the temporary absence of Mr. Stones, the manager, from the counter, the prisoner en- tered the shop and picked up the suit of clothes which were wrapped in a bundle. He tore off the pawn ticket • which was attached, and upon Mr. Stones returning into the shop the prisoner quickly re-pawned them. He was , afterwards apprehended by P.C. Maitland, whom he in- , formed he had enjoyed himself in spending the money he had obtained. The prisoner was sentenced to a month's ' hard labour, Mr. Gaskell remarking that he was sorry he could not order him to be dogged.

WIDNIS Antsartc CLUB SPORTS.—These annual sports will take place on Friday and Saturday next, and 'favoured with fine weather, will maintain the reputation gained as the most important and enjoyable fixture of its kind in the North of England. • RUNCORN SCHOOL BOAR'S AT WORK.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the following persons were sum- moned by the Runcorn School Board for not sending their children regularly to school :—Joseph Woocjs, Bridgewater-at. ; William Okell, Cooper-st. ; James Rob- inson, Surrest-st. • John Powell, Vine-at.; Jos. Wakefield, Granville-st: ; George Lydiate, Surrey-st. ; Thos.Horton, Gilbert-st. ; George Richardson, Wellington-st. ; Thomas Lucas, Bridgewater-at. ;William Salkeld, Norton-st. ; and Mary Burke, Brunswick-st. The cases were proved by Mr. Bowyer, and the usual fine of 5s was imposed in each instance. WILFUL DAMAGE AT RUNCON.M.—WaIter Hazlehurst, a youth, and Ernest Ford, a boy. were summoned to Run- corn Petty Sessions on Monday, charged with wilfully damaging, to the extent of 10s, a wall at the Ferry Hut, belonging to the Bridgewater Trustees. The charge against Ford was withdrawn. William Leach, policeman to the trustees, prodtel the case, and said the amount of damage done by such youths as the defendant was very heavy. The sum of would not cover what had been done by the defendant and his companions on the 27th ' Ma. the defendant was ordered to pay 184 6d, or go • to gaol for Seven days. ROB GEO A lIIIANDFATIIER AT RUNCORN.—nefOre Mr. A. Thomas, at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, Samuel Thompson, a young man, who follows the occupation of • a joiner, was charged with stealing £5O 4s belonging to his grandfather, Mr. Samuel White, of Greenway-road. The money and cash box was missed from the house on Monday evening, and as the prisoner, who lived with his • grandfather, was also missing, suspicion fell upen him, and information was given to the police. Inspector O'Donnell traced the culprit tothe Mersey Hotel, Widnes, where he apprehended him on Tuesday morning, whilst he was taking his breakfast. The stolen money was found in his possession The prisoner was remanded for a week. • THE WIDOW'S COMPLAINT. —. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, an old woman, named Ennis Lewis, who said she was a widow and lived at Ditton, complained that a man named William Mizzen had broken into her dwelling by unlawful means. She was away for the good of her health at the time. She alleged that the man had wrenched two locks off the door, stolen the copy of a will, broken a big jug, and many other articles were missing.—lnspector Keighley said the woman had been at the police station on about ten occasions making a eimilar complaint, and it was thought that she was the victim of some nervous derangement.—The woman said she was breaking her heart over the matter, and Mr. Less in (magistrate's clerk) promised that inquiries should be made. A VIOLENT CUSTOMER AT RUNCORN.—Peter Harris, a rough-looking young fellow, was brought before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. J. Brundrit, at Runcorn Court, .on Wednesday morning, charged with having been drunk in the Boathouse-Inn, Mersey-st., and refusing to quit when requested by the landlord, Thomas Finegan. About four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon the prisoner entered the house and asked for a drink. The landlord thought he had had sufficient, and refused to supply him. The prisoner then acted its a very violent fe.shion, and pul- ling off his clog damaged the counter. The landlord ejected him into the street, whereupon the prisoner pulled off his other clog, and sent it through a window worth 10s. He was taken into custody by P.C. Jackson, and was now fined 20s and costs or a month. He went to gad. INVADING THE SALVATION ARMY PREMISES AT RUN- coßN.—llalph Warren, a respectable-looking, middle- aged man, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday, charged with having on Sunday, the third June, been, with intent to commit a felony, on premises occupied by " Captain" Walbron, at the Salvation Army Barracks. About one o'clock on Sunday morning the lieutenant at the " barracks " heard a noise in the yard, and awakened the captain. The latter having procured a light, went inehe yard and found the prisoner crouched in a corner. The captain sounded a whistle, and Dr. McDougall opened his bedroom window. Learning what was the matter, Dr. McDougall gave an alarm, which brought P.C. Gibson on the scene, and the prisoner was given in charge.—The prisoner said he was in drink at the time, and he did not know what could have taken him into the yard unless he was inquiring for lodgings. —He was fined lOs and costs or 14 days' hard labour, and was told he must be careful where he went at that time of the night. AN Ecceerrine ENGINE-DRIVER.—At the Altrincham Petty Sessions, on Monday. before Mr. W. Armitage and other magistrates, John Kinsey, an engine-driver, be- longing to Widnes, was charged with stealing a set of dominoes, value 3s 6d, and a pint pot, the property of William Millyard, Bull's Head Inn Lymm. Mr. Cave defended, and the prisoner pleaded "not' guilty." The evidence was to the effect that on the 29th May prisoner went to the Bull's Head and asked if a man was there with whom he had been in company on the previous night. He was told he was not there, whereupon he went through the kitchen into the yard. A waiter served him with a pint of beer in the kitchen. The samerevening John Whitfield, a labourer, saw the pri- soner put something down in a field, and on going to the edace he found a pint pot with a set of dominoes.—For , the defence Mr. Cave contended that it was while under the effects ofdrink that he took the pint pot and the dominoes, and hid them in the field. When under the influence of drink prisoner's manner was very peculiar, and seeing that he had been in custody since the previous Tuesday, Mr. Cave held that the ends of justice had been vindicated. Evidence was called in support of this statement, and the case was finally dismissed.—Prisoner was further charged with stealing a half-sovereign, the property of Thomas Brooks„ at LYmm, on the 20th May, but after hearing the evidence the magistrates dismissed , this charge also. = WARNING TO Doe Owtans AT RUNCOANi-11efore ‘Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Evans, Ship Canal labourer, William Findley Coope, 3, Handley-st., and Henry Price, boatman, of Canal-st., were each fined Is, and costs 9s 6d, for allowing their dogs to be at large un- muzzled.—William Littler, insurance agent. Duke's-field, was charged with having his dog insecurely muzzled on the 25th May. Constables Breeze and Hulse stated that they saw the dog at Higher Runcorn in- charge of the defendant's son, who was accompanied by his uncle. The dog had a muzzle fixed on its head, but it was of no use whatever, and the animal could have bitten anybody. The uncle said it was quite sufficient if the dog had a muzzle on. The defendant positively asserted that the dog could not bite, and argued that the fact' of the dog having a muzzle on showed that he had no wish to break the law. Super- intendent Hollingvrorth said they could not pro- perly muzzle a dog with the straps defendant had, with- out cruelty to the-animal. Dog owners should get wire muzzles, which allowed the dog to open its mouth but prevented it from biting. Mr. A. Thomas : And most dangerous things they are too. The Bench did not think. defendant intended to break the law and dismissed the summons. He was warned to keep the dog securely muzzled in futures—John Price, grocer, halton-road; was summoned on a similar charge, and he was also dis- missed. THE TERRIBLE ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. H. Gaskell, junr., James Duggan. labourer, High-st., was again brought up charged with having on the 26th May in- flicted grievous bodily harm upon his wife. Julia.—Mr. Lewin, magistrates clerk, read a certificate from Dr. Hutchinson, who said the injured woman was not quite out of danger, and a correct opinion of her case could not be formed for a fortnight.—Superintendent Johnston therefore asked that the prisoner should be remanded for a week. At this moment MrseDuggan appeared in court, and stated that she felt "all right," and she asked His Worship to proceed with the case. She denied that her husband had assaulted' her and alleged that the injuries from which she had suffered were self inflicted. She wished her husband to" get off," because if he were kept in gaol much longer, the house would have to be broken up and the children sent to the workhouse.—Mr. Lewin pointed out that the woman in her de,sposition, taken when she thought she was going to die, distinctly swore that her husband committed the assault.—Mrs. Duggan replied, that when she gave that evidence she was not in her right mind, and Dr. Hutchinson could say that she did not recover consciousness until the following Tuesday.—Superintendent Johnston said the woman had been very seriously injured and did not rise from her; bed until Saturday.—The prisoner stated that he " never rose his hand" to his wife in his life.—Mr. Gaskell said he could not go into the facts that day, and remanded the prisoner for a week. WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.—Thursday, before Mr. H. Gasket'. senr., and Mr. F. H. Gossage.—Druak and Dis- orderly : For this offence the following persons were each fined 5s and costs :—George Jenkinson, Mill-brow; CI-Arles Manning, Mill-brow; and Thomas Hogan, Harrison-St., Ditton.—James Hardman, of 74, Lugs- dale-road, was charged on the evidence of P.C. Evans with causing a breach of the peace in Victoria-road by ' fighting with another man who made his escape: After hearing the evidence the defendant was dismissed.— Trespassers in Trouble: Joseph Gill, Henry Wright, William Punter, and Robert Galilee, youths, were sum- moned for trespassing upon a field in the occupation of Henry Baker, farmer, Ditton, and with committing damage to the grass by tramping it down. They were , ordered to pay costs.—School Board Cases: The follow- , ing were each finod 6d and 4s 6d costs for not sending their children to school regularly :—Patrick MePartland, Peter McCafferty, Hugh Cosgrove, Pat. Daley, Pat. Huelies, Joseph Lithstoo, Charles Mac Kenna, Alice Wylde, William Houghton, Jemes Carr, Christopher Cockerman, Jomipli Parkes, Ellen Roche, Dennis Malone, and Michael Glynn. Mr. Denby appeared on behalf of the School Board.—Horse Astray: Thomas Edwardson was sum- moned at the instance of P.C. Foster for allowing a bay mare to stray in Albert-road. He was fined 2s 6d and 4s 6d costs.—Themeing Stones: Peter Illidge, 17, Oakland- st., and John McCormick, 34, Water-st., were both charged with throwing stones in Waterloo-road, to the danger of passers by. Defendants were each fined is and 4s costs.—Dogs at Larye: For not keeping their dogs under proper control a fine of 5s and costs was imposed upon each of the following :—Joseph Tharme, Henry Lewes, Wm. Higginson, Albert Russell, Wm. Leather- barrow, and Wilbraham Wood.

HALTON PAROCHIAL eHILDRRN'S SICK CLUB.—The re- port of this club shows that there are 88 members, and that the amount suscribed last year was £l4 5s 100. The payments to sick members amounted to £lO ss. There was a total credit balance of £132 15s 2d. THE MANOMETER MunnEntn.--Constable Thompson on Tuesday observed a man loitering about the streets of Widnes, and as he bore a strong resemblance to the notorious Jackson he took him to the police station. The man stated that lie was a bricklayer in search of 'employment, and as he (lid not bear the marks stated to be on Jackson he was set at liberty. DISORDERLYCHAILACTERS AT RUNCORN.—Elizabeth Bird, Alice Johnson, Margaret Jones (" Welsh Mag ") and Ellen Whitty, all women of ill-fame, were brought before the Runcorn magistrates yesterday charged with in- decent conduct. Inspector O'Donnell and Sergeant Woolley proved the charges, and each prisoner was sea- tencen to a month's hard labour.

A VIOLENT RAILWAY PASSENGER AT WIDNES. At Widnes Court, on Thursday, James Miles, of no settled residence, was charged with having on Tuesday, travel- ' led from St. Helens to Widnes without having pre- viously paid his fare • also with being drunk and asleep in the carriage, and further with assaulting P.C. Woes- fold. Upon the train arriving at Widnes from St. Helens, the prisoner tendered a ticket from Skelmersdale to St. Helens, and refused to pay the difference or to re- turn to St. Helens. He commenced to abuse the ticket collector, and P.C. Worsfold was called ia. Theprisoner struck that officer a violent blow on Op+ face. For travel- ling without ticket the prisoner was fined les and costs, 8s ed. The other charges were withdrawn, as the priso- ner had been in prison sbveral days. SMUGGLING AT RUNCORN.—AIbert Winslade, mate of r the schooner Sarah McDonald, was brought before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. J. Brundrit, at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, charged with smuggling 11b. of coven- dish tobacco and 11b. 14oz. of cigars. Mr. Mitchell, superintendent of customs, prosecuted. The schooner arrived at the port on Thursday from Jersey, and Mr. T. Garner, one of the Custom House officiaLs, boarded the vessel. The prisoner said there was only half a lb. of tobacco on board, but Mr. Garner found the quantity named in the charge concealed in a false compartment of the mate's cabin. The defendant said he had brought the tobacco and cigars for a friend.—He pleaded guilty, and was fined £3 9s 4d, being double value and duty, to- gether with costs 8s led SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES YOUTII.—At the Widnes Petty Sessioni. on 'Thursday, before Mr. Hol- brook Gasket!, William Kinsdla, a youth, was charged on remand with wounding John Moffatt, a labourer. Prosecutor alleged that do the night of the 22nd ult, he was going along Brynn-st. with his o)usin, when they saw a crowd of boys with some of whom his cousin quarrelled. Complainant was about to go to his assis- tance when the father of the prisoner came out of his house and struck him. At the same time the prisoner commenced to throw stones at him, some if which struck Moffatt on the head. The prosecutor was taken to Dr. O'Keefe, when he was foundto be suffering from a lacera- ted wound on the right cheekbone' a black eye, and a second lacerated wound on the back of the head which penetrated to the bone. The inan vsits not yet well, and could not follow his employment. 'Prisoner was commit- ted to the sessions for trial. .

- LIVELY' SCENE AT A lIIINCORN JEWELLER'S Saw.—Be fore Mr. A. Thomas and Major Ha.zlehurst, at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, John Smith, a tramping shoe- maker, was charged with being drunk and diserderly. On the previous evening the prisoner entered the shop of Mr. J. B. Bankes, watchmaker and jeweller, High-st., axd demanded money. Upon being refused he acted in a most violent and threatening fashion. He was thump- ing with his fist a glass case containing valuable jewel- lery, when Mr. Frank Johnson and Mr. James Collier ap- peared on the scene, and the latter gentleman, (who is brother-in-law to Mr. Bankes), put the prisoner into the street. The prisoner then attempted to smash the shop window, but was prevented, and he afterwards seized Mr. Bankes by the throat and threatened to wreak dire vengeance upon him. :Several bystanders took charge of the prisoner until the arrival of a constable, when he was removed to the cells. The magistrates sentenced the prisoner to a month's hard labour in default of paying a fine of 2s and costs.

_„.„... A Row AMONGST THE NAVVIES AT RUNCOEN.—At Run- corn Police Court, on Wednesday, before Major Hanle- burst and Mr. A. Thomas, six navvies named John Christie, William Simmons, Henry Spring, George Hughes, Charles Davies, and Alfred Webster, were , charged with being drunk and disorderly in Church-st., on the previous night. Several witnesses gave evidence ! that about eleven o'clock on Wednesday night the pri- soners created a great disturbance in Church-st., and a! large crowd assembled. They were observed to knock another navvy down and kick him in a most cruel fashion. It was thought that the man's knee was broken, but the doctor pronounced that the limb was badly bruised. Apparently glad to have escaped so easily the man said it did not matter if it was only a bruise. Supt. Hollingworth asked the Bench to show their opinion of this outrageous conduct by imposing a heavy penalty. Each defendant was fined 20s, and costs 8s 4d, or 21 days' hard 140ur.-4ohn Beddow, of Widnes, for being. drunk and disorderly in Church-st., on the previous night, was fined 10s and costs.—A sailor named Murdoch McDonald was fined 5s and costa for being drunk. STARTLING SIPTDENCE IN TEM SALT DISTRICT. —On Tu-Aday morning the workmen employed at Mr. Earlam's chairlactory at North wich were greatly terrified by seeing the floor of one of the sheds give way. A huge pit was instantaneously formed, and a large number of chairs and implements were en- gulfed. The subsidence is all the more startling as the immediate locality has hitherto I.ren considered safe.

A ISEW POSTCARP.—Thoio " Daily News ' says the Postmaster-Oener.il has under Inc consideration a fieW kind of clo;NI p.-,g,:!ard, which will have the privacy cf a letter, and will be sold at something less than the price of a penny stamp. Mr.. Raikes is, we have reason to believe, so far favourable to the experiment that the cards will shortly be issued to the public. SMALLPDX IN ST. lIELENS.—ABOther 0.80 of smallpnx has been discovered in St. Helens. John Hargreaves, 20 years of age. a collier from Wigan, was admitted into the Infections Diseases Hospital on Monday suffering from the diseaee. The sufferer said he came from Wigan about a week ago, and had been staying in a lodging-house on Greenbank at night, but during the day he had been out look- ing for work. TOTAL ABSTINENCE LEAGUE OF THE CROSS.--At a well-attended and enthusiastic meeting of the parishioners of St. Edward's Church. Runcorn, held in the Schoolroom. on Sunday, it was unanimously resolved to establish a Catholic Total Abstinence League of the Cross at Runcorn As many as 55 members at once took the pledge. After the meet- ing.a lecture was given by Mr. D. Houghton, presi- dent of the Warrington branch, to the members, in which he strongly exhprted them to keep the pledge. The meeting was brought to a close by a vote of thanks to the president. and lecturer. Tint HomE IRON TRADE. There is some im- provement in the English iron market this week, although the amount of trade is not meet) larger. The aspect in the pig-iron market has been some- what more cheerful, which is partly due to the better shipments recorded for May, partly to • the consequent reduction in stocks of Cleveland iron, and partly also to the greater buoyancy in the Glas- gow warrant market. Notwithstanding this latter fact, however, the price of Scotch makera' iron has declined from 3d to is per ton on the week. Mid- dlesbrough pig No. 3 is 31 per ton higher, and Bes- semer pig has also gene up 6d.—lron. THE.ST. lIELF.NS NEW RAILWAY.—At a meeting of the directors of the new St. Helens Railway Com- pany, on Wednesday afternoon, the Chairman (Mr. henry Set•on-Karr. M.P.), who presided, said he had made an inspection of the works at Golborne, and was thoroughly satisfied with all he had seen, and with the spirited way in which proress was being made by Mr. Pilling, the contractor. The first !fee- tion extends from Lowton Junction to the llaydeck Collieries, and a large number of men were now en- gaged on it. The question of immediately com- mencing work in St. Helens was introduced and warmly received, and it was decided to ask Mr. Pilling to at once report on the inatter,with the view of making a start on the Greenongh estate in Parr, through which the line will run. EDWARD YOUNG. AND COMPANY, LIMITED—On Thursday, the 14th inst., the subscription list for this CoMpany will be opened, and will be closed on or before Saturday first, the 10th, and the Liverpool Commercial Banking Company, Limited, Liverpool, and William Deacon and Company, London, are authorised to receive applications for shares. The share capital is £150,000, in 15,000 shares of ..£lO each, and .C 75,000 five per cent. debentures. The present issue is 8,500 ordinary shares and £45,000 debentures—in all, £l3o,ooo—of which applications have been received for over £BO,OOO before the registration of the company. This company has been formed for thepurpose of acquiring the business of Edward Young and Co., Liverpool, distillers, recti- tiers,manufactuers of cordials and wholesale wine and spirit merchants. The business was established over seventy years ago, and throughout this period a steady and profitable trade has been consistently maintained. The existing business arrangements will be altered as little as possible, the two present partners having undertaken to continue the man- agement, and the whole of the staff being retained. The books have been examined by Messrs, Cochrane and Walker, chartered accountants, Liverpool, whose report shows that after providing for deben- ture interest the average profits of the last four years, and also for the last twenty years, have been sufficient to pay a dividend of 10 per cent, per an- num on the present issue of shares. The profits for the first four months of this year shew more than sufficient to pay the same dividend.

VIOLENT STRUGGLE WITH A LUNATIC. OR _

Saturday afternoon, a man named Charles Price, who was said to have come from Cardiff, but lately living at Latchford. was brought before Mr. T. P. Norris at the Lymm Police Court, on a charge of lunacy. Price had first been apprehended for com- mitting damage on Mr. R. A. Naylor's premises at Thelwall. On being brought into court he made an attempt to assault Sergeant Harrington, and while in the court room he behaved in a most violent

manner. He made a desperate attempt to get hold of the fender, but was prevented by the police, and shortly afterwards he made a rapid spring at the fire grate and wrenched out the bars. Those pre- sent, of course, attempted to disarm him, and there ensued a violent struggle in the room, but eventu- ally, and not without great effort, Price was hand- cuffed. He was afterwards taken to Macclesfield Asylum in a cab, his legs haying to be tied on the way.
NEW MISSION ROOM AT PRESTON BROOK.—An inaugural tea meeting has been held in the Mission Room at Preston Brook which has lately been

built by Sir Gilbert Greene' 11 for the benefit Of those who live in this quarter of the parish of Daresbury, and which for the last few weeks has been open for service on Sunday. Sir Gilbert, however, owing to his recent illness, was unable te attend that even-

ing, but Lady oreenall and her daughters were present. The proceedings began at six o'clock with a substantial tea, to which upwards of 200 sat down, and appeared to do ample justice to the good things provided or them. Shortly after tea the second part of the evening's entertainment com- menced, when, after a few words of address by the Rev. T. Whitley and Mr. McWhanall, a capital pro- gramme of music and comic songs was gone through, and listened to by a most appreciative audience. The Misses Greenall both received a

hearty encore, as, indeed, was the case with each one of those who so kindly contributed to render the evening a most enjoyable one, and which was brought to a close by singing the National Anthem, in which all present heartily joined. THE ATTEMPTED SUICIDE IN A RAILWAY CAR- RIAGE.—IIenry Whitehead, a young married man, whose father lives at Manchester, was brought be- fore Mr. A. Sinclair and Mr. A. Walmsley, at the St. Helens Town Hall. on Wednesday, charged under remand with attempting to commit suicide in a railway carriage in which he was travelling from Manchester to Liverpool, on the night of the 28th ult. On the arrival of the train at St. Helens June-

tion, at 8-8 p.m., prisoner was found insensible, tied to the rack with his pocket-handkerchief, which had beenpassed round his neck. He was cut down, and:taken to tho Providence Hospital, where he re- covered. Prisoner has been in Walton Gaol for a week. Prisoner then said that he arrived from America three weeks since, and found that his mother had been dead twenty-four hours. Previous toigoing to America he had a good character for honesty and sobriety, and had testimonials from the Mayor and leading gentlemen of Beverley. Ile never in all his life premeditated doing such an act as he had done. It was purely through drink. A week in gaol had been a lesson he should never forget. Ile was very sorry indeed for what he had done. It was all through drink, and if the magistrates would let him go he would go to his wife and never taste drink again as long as he lived. The Bench discharged the prisoner and hoped it would be a warning to him. . _

WARRINGTON FARMERS' CUM.—A meeting of the committee of this club was held on Wednesday evening, at the Farmers' Stores, Mr. J. Percival pre- siding. The subject of the sale of foreign for Eng- lish meat was again introduced, and the discussion was of a similar nature to the one that took place at a recent meeting, which was reported at the time. Mr. T. Dutton said that they must maintain the position that they had talten up on this question. It was only the " fradulent " sale of foreign meat that they took exception to. Mr. W . Darbsh ire said the main object of the action of the club was to show that a large quantity of foreign meat of an inferior quality was sent to England, where it was sold as English meat. An Act of Parliament similar to the one in force regulating the sale of butter was required in regard to the sale of meat. Mr. J. L. Stelfox said that a let of animals, that had either died or were about to die of disease in other coun- tries, were sent to England and passed off on un- witting customers as home-fed meat. He could not conceive how any family butcher doing an honest trade could take the least exception to the action of the club. A letter that had been received from the Wirral Farmers' Club was rea4l, It stated that the club bad resolved that the Chester and Warrington farmers should be asked to appoint gentlemen to meet two gentlemen appointed by the Wirral club for the purpose of drawing up a combined resolution of the three clubs on the question of the sale of foreign meat, with a view to the prevention of such sale. It was decided that Messrs. J. Percival and J, L. Stelfox be appointed a deputation as requested. The meeting then proceeded to consider the recom- mendation of the Central Dairy Farmers' Associa- tion to establish factories after the manner of the Rocester Cheese Factory. After a short discussion the subject dropped, and the meeting, after con- sidering the proposed Tithes Variation Bill, was brought to a conclusion. A WIDNES MIN'S VISIT TO WARRINGTON.—At the Borough Court at Warrington yesterday morn- ing, a man named Hugh Daley, a tin-plate worker, Bank-st., was brought up on remand on a charge of having stolen from the shop of Frederick Jenkins, 94, Bridge-st., a pair of boots, value Bs. Od. He was also charged with having stolen from the person of ,Jeales Bibby, Kent-st., Simms Cross, Widnes, on Irsiresday, in Winwick-st., a silver watch, steel guard, and pocket knife, value 198., or of having received the same knowing them to have been stolen. With regard to the first charge, evidence was given to the effect that the boots were missed, information was given to the police, and when pursuing inquiries into the matter Constable Monaghan met prisoner wearing them. The circumstances of the second • case were to the effect that on Saturday Bibby, who is employed at the works of Messrs. Sullivan and Company, Widnes, came to Warrington with the articles named in the charge in his possession. Dur- ing the evening lie got drunk, and at about four o'clock on Sunday morning he awoke to find that, he had been sleeping on some steps in Winwick-st. His hat, watch, chain, and knife were gone. Bibby reported the matter to the police, and it was ascer- tained that on Monday morning prisoner offered the watch and chain in pledge, but the pawnbroker, not being satisfied with the answers prisoner gave to various westions, refused to take it in. When in eustody dii the first charge, prisoner was ques- tioned with regard to the watch, and said that it was his own' and he had sold it. The man whom he said had bought it, however, said that he was only taking care of the watch. On being formally charged with stealing the watch, chain, and knife, prisoner said that at two o'clock on Sunday morn- ing a man gave them to him in Winwick. After the articles had been identified, and other evidence given, the magistrates sent Daley to prison for two months, with hard labour.

div.head: DrTY OF THE PRESS. (From the "South Birmingham News.")
div.p: THE DrTY OF THE PRESS. (From the "South Birmingham News.")

If there is any special duty which falls to the lot of the Press, it is to commend and endorse that which is discovered to be meritorious and worthy, whether it be concerning persons or things. A strik- ing illustration of this duty of commending the truly valuable has just come under our notice, and is here published for the benefit of our readers. "At 18, Lower Pazeley-st., Birmingham, lives Mr. W. Long, a smart-looking young man under thirty years of age, with a remarkably bright and intelli- gent face. Mr. Long is employed at Mr. Lyndon's spade manufactory in Birmingham, His usual work isjwhat is technically known as " facing,' and he also does 'drawing," which is a very laborious occupation, and necessitates exposure to great heat. Ever since last autumn the work there has been very busy, and the hands have been working overtime. The long hours, hard work, and extreme heat to which Mr. Long was subject finally proved too much of a strain, and he was taken ill. He lost all spirit, his mouth be- came badly ulcerated, and he suffered from excruciating pains in the back. Speaking of his recovery Mr. Long said—' One day while sitting at home a man left a little book, and having nothing to do just then I began to read it. I soon got interested and determined to give War- ner's SAFE Cure a trial, being convince that if it did me no good, it could do me no harm. I commenced taking it in small doses three times a day, and soon perceived it was doing me good in several ways. I had more spirit and less pain, my appetite returned, and I felt much better in every way. I continued with the medicine and was very soon a different man. I can work to-day and as well and with as little fatigue as ever I could in my life, and I owe my recovery to Warner's SAYS Cure.' , Such is the story of Mr. Long as related by him to the editor of the News,'" The world is full of people who are suffering from the same great evil which undermined his he alth. Mr. Long felt it his duty to reveal the means that restored him to health, and the editor of this paper believes it is clearly his duty, as an educator of the people, to make this case known to the public.

Total RUNCORN V. CHESTER Tows.—Since the Runcorn club opened the season they have scored an unbroken list of successes. Six matches have been played and won, and supporters of the summer game are buoyed up with hope that the town will take the prominent position in the cricket world which it occupied about 16 years ago. Mr. Cleorge Ward, the relieving officer, has just made an interesting presentation to the club. He bad in his pos- session a bat which was used by William Elliott in the compilation of large scores, when he was the professional to the Cricket Club in its palmiest days. This bat he has handed to the club, and by his wish it will be presented to the highest scorer at Gatley's benefit match, which is to take place shortly. On Saturday the eleven played Chester Town at Runcorn, and won easily by seven wic- kets. Mr. McCregon, a new resident in the town made a most successfnl first appearance in the team He is a player of scientific attainments, and by sterling cricket he compiled a score of 40. THE SHIP CANAL WORKS,
AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.

No. 21.—THE BRIDGEWATER CANAL. Though Runcorn boasts a record which runs back into the dim beginnings of national history, its modern importance is mainly due to the making of the Bridgewater Canal, of which it is the western terminus, just as we may anticipate that its greater ' future will be largely owing to the construction of the Ship Canal. The Bridgewater Canal, which in its day was perhaps an even more notable under- taking than the Ship Canal is now, was projected about the middle of last century by the Duke of Bridgewater, to provide a cheap means of carrying coal from his mines to Manchester. and in 1758 and 1759 an Act was obtained "for enabling his grace to cut a canal from Worsl ey to Salford, near Manches- ter, and to carry the same to or near Rollin Ferry, in the county of Lancaster." It was, however, after- wards decided to vary the course of the canal, and it was carried over the Irwell by the famous aqueduct designed and carried out by the untaught genius of Brindley, in the face of the ridicule and predictions of failure of the "highest authorities" of the time. In 1762 the duke sought and obtained Parliamentary sanction for extending his canal to the Mersey, and, says Smiles in his "Lives of the Engineers, "when, this deviation was proposed, the bold imagination of Brindley projected a bridge across the tideway of the Mer- sey itself, which was then some four hun- dred and sixty yards wide, with the object of carrying the Duke's navigation directly onward to the port of Liverpool on the Lancashire side of the river." This project seems to have been earnestly pressed by Brindley, and in a Liverpool paper of the time we find the following passage —"On: Monday last, Mr. Brindley waited upon several of the prin- cipal gentlemen of this town and others at Run- corn, in order to ascertain the expenses that may attend the building or a bridge over the River Mer- sey at the latter place, which is estimated at a sum inferior to the advantages that must arise both to the counties of Lancaster and Chester from a com- munication of this sort." The great scheme, was, however, in the end abandoned, and the work of spanning the Igersey at Runcorn was left to the Werra; of a later day. A CONTEMPORARY ACCOUNT. The feelings with which the progress of the canal was watched at the time are disclosed in some con- temporary references, chief amongst these being a letter, not without literary merits, written from Warrington on the Ist January, 1773. "The Duke of Bridgewater's Canal Navigation, which has," says the writer, "drawn the attention and excited the admiration of the curious from all parts, is , now passable for boats, between Manchester and • the river Mersey, at Runcorn (except where for the space of about one mile near Sir Richard Brooke's, ' where a difficulty has unhappily arisen about the course in which it .is to be made). The . _ _

fall from the canal into the Mersey is near ninety feet, which within the distance of six hundred yards, is divided into ten locks for vessels of upwards of fifty tons burden. They are admir- ably contrived and supplied with water from the canal through basins and aqueducts formed in rock. These locks have been most skilfully and substantially constructed within a space of nine months, through the amazing abilities and inde- fatigable industry of Mr. John Gilbert, who, with the assistance of the late very ingenious Mr. Brind- ley, first planned, and has conducted this great work to its present successful period. Yesterday the locks were opened, and the Heart of Oak, a vessel from Liverpool, belonging to the Duke, passed through them. This day, upwards of six hundred of his Grace's workmen were entertained upon the lock banks with an ox roasted whole, and plenty of good liquor. The Duke's health and many other toasts were drunk, with the loudest acclama- tions from the multitude, who crowded from all parts of the country to be spectators of these as- tonishing works; and everything was conducted with the greatest order and propriety. The gen- tlemen of the country for a long time entertained a very unfavourable opinion of this undertaking, es- teeming it too difficult to be accomplished, and fearing their lands would be cut and defaced, with- out producing any real benefit to themselves or the public; but they now see with pleasure that their fears and apprehensisons were ill-groninded ; and i join with one voice n applauding the work, which cannot fail to produce the most beneficial conse- quences to the landed property,as wellas to the trade and commerce of this part of the kingdom. It is the universal wish of the country that the only re- maining obstacle to the completion of this stupen- dous work may be speedily removed, and that the 'dispute between his Grace and Sir Richard Brooke

may be amicably adjusted, without the trouble, 'expense, and delay of another application to Par- liament; as, we are informed. if that was settled, the remaining part of the navigation might be com- pleted in a few weeks, and the public eased of an expense of one shilling and eight pence per ton, which must be paid for the land carriage of goods over that intermediate space of ground until the boats can pass through it. We are at a loss whether to admire the nol4le spirit and intrepidity of the Duke in undertaking this arduous work or his for- titude and manly perseverance in the execution of it, under all the difficulties and impediments which have fallen in his way. It must be added to the honour of his Grace that there never was a work, either public or private, better conducted, or carried on with greater order and regularity in the execu- tion, or punctuality in respect of payments, nor with less cause of complaint than this has been." Also, we find in the "Gentleman's Magazine" for January 1766, "An entertaining description of the Duke of Bridgewater's surprising navigable canal," with an engraved plan of the waterway as it then was. This account remarks that from Stretford the canal "will probably be extended to the Mersey, as far as Liverpool; and if so, what a most noble con- venience will this be for travellers. We should then travel with as much certainty, pleasure, and dis- patch as in the treekscuits in Holland and Flanders —and if the boats were covered, we might travel by night or day, and sleep, read, write, play at cards, drink tea, and partake of many diversions."

WARRINGTON (2ND ELIIVRN) V. GOLBORNE.—PIayed at Warrington on Saturday. and resulted in a win for the visitors by 13 runs and 8 wickets to fall. For the visitors and Bradburn showed the best cricket, and for the home team Adamson and Sutton rendered valuable aid. div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The English football team played a match against a local fifteen at Bathurst, on Wednesday, in the presenc3 of some 5,000 spectators. Some good play was shown on both sides, the visitors eventually winning by a goal and four tries to three tries. .

At Nottingham on Tuesday the Australian cricketers sustained their third defeat within a fortnight, Notts beating them in a decisive fashion by ten wickets. The record of their tour now stands thus :—Five matches won, three lostrand one drawn. The reverse on Tues- day was a severe one, but Jones and M‘Donnell, the two best batsmen on the side were away. All the same, the Notts men deserve immense credit for their victory. After a thoroughly interesting day's cricket, in which fortune favoured each county in turn, Lancashire beat Middlesex, amidst great excitement, by 24 runs at Lords on Tuesday. There was some good cricket on Thursday. Lancashire had all the best of the day's play in their match with Gloucestershire. The latter went in first, and, owing to the fine bowling of Barlow and Briggs, were all out for 48. The Lancashire men scored 232 for eight wickets, F. Sugg being not out with 102 to his credit. On the same day Middlesex ran up a score of 317 against Nats, and seven of the team reached good double figures.

div.head: CELEBRATIONS.
div.p: CELEBRATIONS.

The canal was completed in 1776, the total cost of its construction from Worsley to Manchester, and from Longford Bridge to the Mersey at Runcorn amounting to £220,000. The opening of the Run- corn portion of the canal was celebrated, amongst other ways, by the drinking of th following toasts which illustrate how conservative we are in the form of our toast lists.
The King, Queen, and Royal Family. The Duke of Bridzewater, and success to the Navigation. General Cholinondeley, Lord of the Manor of Runcorn. Mr. John Gilbert.
All the honest fellows who have exerted themselves
_ in the execution of these works. Prosperity to trade and navigation. Prosperity to thd town of Runcorn. THE ENGINEER OF THE SCHEME.

The highest wage he received whilst in the employ- ment of the duke was 3s Gd a day. For the greater 'part of the time he received only half a crown." It ' is said of Brindley that on one occasion, when giv- ing evidence before a committee of the House of Commons, he spoke very disparagingly of rivers and their facilities for navigation. One of the members of the committee asked him for what pur- pose he imagined rivers had been created, and after a few moments deliberation, Brindley replied with great gravity that "Rivers were made for the purpose of feeding navigable canals." This in its way was as good a reply as that often-told one of a kindred genius. deorge Stephenson, who, when catechised by a House of Commons committeeman, as to what would be the result if a cow got in front of his locomotive, retorted that it would be bad for the " coo "
