The Primitive Methodist Conference was opened in Liverpool, on Wednesday. The Rev. T. Whittaker, of that city, was elected president for the ensuing year. PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY.—Among the crew of the ill-fated Cunard steamer Demerara, which was lost with all hands, were nine men who had insurance poli- cies with the Prudential Assurance Company. The re- latives of these have received over £4OO, and a no- ticeable feature/is that, with one exception' no policy had been in force two years. No doubt one reason so many insured with the Prudential office is on account of no extra premium beingrequired for mariner's risk.

SPECIAL MEETING. An extraordinary meeting of the sharel.olders of the Manchester Ship Canal Company was held on Monday, at St. Sames's Oxford-st.;to consider the provisions of the bill now before Parliament for the purpose of "altering certain works authorised by the Manchester Ship Canal Act, 1885, and to alter the boundaries between the townships of Stretford and Salford and the borough of Salford and the dis- trict of the Local Board of Stretford, and other pur- pose-:' There was a large attendance of share- holders. In the absence of the Chairman of the Company Lord Egerton of Tatton), the chair was occupied by Sir J. C. Lee, deputy chairman of the Corapany, and amongst those on the platform were Mr. W. H. Bailey, Mr. J. K. Bythell, Mr. W. J. Crossley, Mr. C. J. Galloway, and Mr. Henry Bod- dington, directors of the Company; Mr. E. L. Williams, engineer; Mr. W. J. Saxon. solicitor; Mr. A. H. Whitworth, secretary; Mr. A. M. Dunlap, land agent; Mr. T. A. Walker, contractor; Mr. Mar- shall Stevens, Mr. Thomas Bradford, Mr. J. G. Cooper, Mr. Theo. Gaddum, Mr. E. Guthrie, Dr. Lund, Mr. J. T. W. Mitchell, Mr. Reuben Spencer, Mr. Bosdin, T. Leech, Mr. W. H. Collier, and Mr. B. Armitage (Sorrel Bank). The Secretary (Mr. Alfred 11. Whitworth) rbad the notice calling the meeting. The Chairman said he must begin by apologising for the absence of the Chairman, Lord Egerton, who had been away from home on account of his health. Refer- ring to the object of the meeting, he proceeded to say that owing to the strong opposition of the late Sir Hum- phrey de Trafford the promoters of the bill of 1885 were unable to lay out this end of the canal on the lines which they thought most desirable in the interests of Man- chester and Salford. They had to place part of the Manchester docks on land covered with buildings occu- pied by working men, which would have entailed on the Company a great cost, as the houses would have had to be erected elsewhere. Early in January the directors entered into neg,otiatlons with the present owner of Traf- ford, a gentleman who took an enlightened view of his responsibilities in connection with the canal and the trade of the district—(applause),—and they agreed to purchase a large portion of his home farm, which would enable them to carry out the improvements named in the bill now before Parliament. The land acquired for wharves underalie new plan would cost £83,000 less. than that which they proposed to abandon.—(Applause.) Out of this sum they proposed to spend £BO,OOO on ex- tended quayage. They would be left with a surplus of £23,000. The exact figures were :—Grand total of the cost of the old works sanctioned by Parliament, £1,041,574. 15s 7d ; cost of the substituted undertakings £1,028.588 7s Bd., or a decrease of £12,988 7s 11d. The area of the water space hi the old plan was Doi acres: in the substituted plan 114* acres—increase 14 acres, or 14 percent; the area of quay space in the old plan, 83 acres; in the substituted plan, 152 acres—increase 69 acres, or 84 per cent; length of quay frontage under the old plan 4 miles, under the new plan 5i miles—increase 1* mile, or about 33 per cent. The whole of the negotia- tions were not completed until May, and as it was neces- sary that the contractor should have possession of the ac- quired land without delay, the directors had applied to Parliament to suspend standing orders and allow the bill to proceed. As all parties concerned in the change were agreed, he saw no prospect of any opposition being suc- cessful. All the proposed new works will be made upon lands which the Company have already purchased, or which the owners have agreed to sell to the Company. The time asked for the completion of the works is the same as that taken for the original works, namely until •August, 1892. With these explanations he begged to move that the shareholders give their consent to the pro- motion of the bill in its present form, or with any altera- tions therein Which Parliament may prescribe and of which the directors may approve.—(Applause.) Mr. J. K. Bythell said he had very great pleasure in seconding the motion, because he believed that the new dock scheme would be of immense benefit to the Com- Pail Instead of putting their money into expensive lands and buildings, what they proposed to do was to, put it into quayage. The docks, as altered, would be capable of accommodating a great anKnlnt of additional traffic. keisail(one of the overseers for Stretford) hoped the day was not far distant when such grand schemes as this would not be harassed by conflicting rating interests, and that the amalgamation would soon take place when we should be united in one grand muni- cipality, and Manchester stand in the proud position of the second city in the kingdom. (Applause.) Mr. J. T. W. Mitchell asked whether it would involve any " extras " to Mr. Walker, because " extras " were a very important item. The Chairman said that all the prices at which Mr. Walker worked were scheduled. On the quays and other works £60,000 additional would be spent. That £60,000 would be got out of the £83,000 which they would save from the land. The motion was then put to the meeting and unani- mously adopted. The Chairman said he felt quite certain the arrange- ments that were now being made were of the best, and would be of very great advantage to the Company, but' they had to contend against a great many people living in Manchester who' were always depreciating the value of their great undertaking. Those men, who might be called croakers—(hcar, hear),---had their own interests to serve. They openly stated on the Stock Exchange that they were not going to buy Ship Canal shares until they were very much reduced in value. (A voice: "They'll never buy them, then.") The shareholders had the power in their own hands in this matter. If they would , lock up their shares, if they would stick to them, they would disappoint all those stock-jobbers who were endeavouring to injure their property. It was only the other week that those people informed the newspapers that Mr. Walker had gone to America, that he was very ill and could not do his work. They further stated that the directors had never produced Mr. Walker, and that 1 he might be a myth. Well, Mr. Walker was with them now—(applause).—and he thought they would admit that he was a very good-looking sort of Englishman, and in sound health. He (the Chairman) did not doubt Mr Walker's capacity to complete the great work in which they had all so great an interest. (Hear, hear.) There was also some unprofessional criticism against which' the Company had to contend. There were a great many men who criticised the work which was belly,6 done in the construction of the canal. They said that the chief engineer of the Company had made some mistake—that there were quicksands and a great amount of hard rock which were never calculated upon. All he could tell them with regard to that was that it was absolutely! false. Mr. Williams's examinations of the strata of the estuary of the Mersey had been most extraordinarily accurate, so much so that the contractor had met with very little difficulty ia his Work, and everything up to the present time had been done without incurring " extras." (Applause.) The last time the shareholders Met, the contractor was just beginning to break ground. There wore then only 400 or 500 men employed. Since that time great progress had been made. There were now employed 56 steam excavators, 73 locomotives, 2,367 waggons, 50 steam cranes, 79 miles of temporary railroad, and 6,000 men. (Applause.) It had always been calculated that Mr. Walker would require to exca- vate one million cubic yards of soil per month in order to be up to time. He had ereat pleasure in informing them that during the month of May the total quantity of rock excavated was 21,371 cubic yards, and of soil excavation 1.009,052, making a total of 1,030,423 cubic yards for the month. As the month included Whit-week, they would see that the work was being kept up to time. With the increased machinery Mr. Walker intended to put down there could be no doubt that ere long those figures would be very materially increased. (Hear, hear.) He could only say, in conclusion, that the shareholders had a magnificent property. They had on the banks of the canal land which was bought at agricultural value— some thousands of acres of land—the value of which would he doubled, trebled, quadrupled in a few years. It was just possible their estimate for land might be ex- ceeded, but not to such an extent as to cause them any trouble in their financial arrangements. He thanked the shareholders for their presence; and he begged to call upon them to give a vote of thanks to their old friend Mr. Reilly for allowing them to meet in that hall free of charge. (Applause.) The motion was seconded by Mr. W. J. Crossley, and adopted. Mr. Walker, who was received with cheers, then rose and said a few words in reply to calls from some of the shareholders. He said that some few weeks ago when he was attacked with a slight indisposition he was very much astonished to find a paragraph in some of the newspapers saying that he was unwell, and that he was going to North America. The report was spread so widely that the agent of the White Star Line wrote to. offer him the very best cabin on board one of their ships. He had been a quiet, hard-working man all his life, and did not like this sort of notoriety, and when he awoke that morning and found himself famous he could not understand it at all. He wrote to the papers saying that he did not propose to go to Aanerica. It was owing to the kindness of the gentlemen before him that he had reached this pitch of fame. They had made him famous by entrusting him with the construction of their great undertaking. He hoped he would not disappoint their expectations. With reference to the figures the chair- man had given them in regard to the progress of the works, lie might say that those figures would be increased 50 per cent. in the course of the next four months, with the exception of the last figure—that relating to the men —which he hoped would be trebled. In the work he had undertaken to do there were 48,000,000 cubic yards of of excavation, besides 6,000,000 cubic yards of rock, and the contract provided for that work being done within 48 months, so that, talingit roundly, there was about a million a month to be excavated. In the 'summer time, however, it was necessary that they should do at the rate of two millions a month, lest they should fall behind in I the winter time. They had already passed the million. They would go on steadily increasing, and before the end of the summer he hoped they would reach the two millions. He thanked them very much for the cordial greeting they had given to his name when it was men- tioded. He hoped that at the end of three and a half years, if it should be so long, when they met on the oc-
• calkon.of the ianal being opened for traffic, they would greet him as cordially. (Applause.) The meeting then terminated.

div.head: EASTHAM AND ELLESMERE PORT.
div.p: EASTHAM AND ELLESMERE PORT.

The section extending from Eastham to Ellesmere Port continues to make rapid progress. Blasting on a large scale is carried on, and some of the rock is being dressed to form a face to the estuary embankment. The hospi- tal, the building of which was commenced on the 25th ult, is now rapidly approaching completion. The buil- ding of the chapel also, is being vigorously pushed on. A movement has been set on foot by the energetic mission- ary, Mr. Oakes, aided by the Officials, to inaugurate a reading-room, where the men can go and spend their evenings either by reading the papers or playing chess, draughts, bagatelle, &c. For this purpose a committee has been formed, the majority of whom are the actual toilers, for it is wisely intended that the men themselves shall take some of the responsibility of keeping up the interest in the movement. It is also intended to start a temperance society in connection with the reading-room, as a counter attraction to the village public-houses. Referring to this section a contemporary says: "Quite a little sensation was created last Friday by a report that the man Jackson had been at work here, and had slipped through the fingers of the watchmen and police. It ap- pears that the night timekeeper was taking the name of a fresh hand, when he noticed a strong resemblance to the description he had just read of Jackson. He also noticed that as soon as he was spoken to he put his loft hand in his pocket; when the timekeeper came round the second time he put his hand again into his pocket and asked for a sub-ticket, which was given him. The timekeeper then went to the watchman and told him to look out for the man when he came for sub at 6 o'clock a.m. ; but it appeared that the 'suspect' tried to sell his sub-ticket for less than its value. Whether he did so and someone else drew the money„ or whether he drew it himself, unobserved, is not known, but he could not be found in the morning, though police and watchmen were looking out for him.

MOORE, Szc. There is nothing of more than usual interest to report this week in connection with the works at Moore, Wal- ton, and the neighbourhood. It is alrribst unnecessary to say that progress is still being made by leaps and bounds, although the showery weather that has recently prevailed may have to some slight eNtent retarded operations. The construction of the powder magazine near Moore has been completed. The steam navvies at Walton are still working away, and are rapidly making a cutting in the direction of Wilderspool. Ahead of the machines labourers are engazed in preparatory work. FATAL ACCIDENT AT BARTON.

On Wednesday afternoon, a fatal accident occurred-to a man named Henry Mitchell, residing at 218, Park-st., Patricroft, who was employed at Barton. It appears that the deceased was sitting on the edge of one of a number of empty waggons drawn by an engine, and whilst descending an incline the engine stopped, and the waggons bumped together. The waggon on which the deceased was sitting being suddenly stopped, he *as thrown off with a jerk and fell amongst the wheels, the last three waggons going over him and killing him in. stantaneously.

div.head: SALFORD.
div.p: SALFORD.

The section fora Salford to Irlam is six miles in length, I and the works will!include the is-a:I9R Id9c.lolthe altlgar tion of the canal and roadway at Barton, Trafford Locks, and the whole of the Manchester and Salford Docks. Be- sides containing these extra works, the cutting itself from Barton to Manchester will be almost half as broad again as the other part of the canal. At Barton there is now a cutting of about Bft. deep, 60ft. wide, and half a mile long, besides smaller excavations. On Stickens Island there is a French steam navvy at Work. Unlike the German navvy, this machine cuts through the hardest of clay with apparent ease. It is built after the style of the German machine, and works with buckets in a similar manner, but the whole of the working parts are much stronger and heavier. It has only been at work one week, and has made an immense cutting 250 to 300 yards in length, and through a clay which expe- rienced men say is the hardest they have. seen. The , makers are Messrs. J. Boulet and Cie, Paris. Near this part will be the Barton Locks, and the course of the river is being altered so as to take the water farther away from the cutting and leave it dry for the foundations of the locks. In the trenches the water is troublesome, but by making provision in time for its removal, it has not caused any stoppage of work. There are three steam pumps at work on this part of the sec- tion. The work to be done at Salford and Manchester is great, and must find employment for thousands of people for some time. On this section there are 1,200 men now working, five steam navvies, and seventeen locomotives; and there are seventeen miles of rails laid. The works at Salford are connected by means of a viaduct and branch line, one-third of a Mile long, with the Midland and Cheshire Lines, which crosses these two railways, the Bridgewater Canal, and River Dwell. THE STORAGE OF EXPLOSIVES.

At the County Petty Sessions at Warrington, on Wed- nesday, Mr. Taylor, C.E., Chester, made an application to the magistrates on behalf of the constructor of the Manchester Ship Canal. It was for permission to build a magazine or store to hold 2,000 lbs. of powder, or 1,000 lbs. of mixed explosives, at a spot near Rixton. It was, he said, proposed to construct a store strictly in accordance with the Act, indeed, Mr. Mialker intended to construct his stores even better than the Act required that he should do. In reply to the chairman of the magistrates (Mr. Edward Greenall), Mr. Taylor said that the store at Moore was finished. The one proposed to be built near Chester would be of a similar character. The application was granted on condition that Mr. Tay- lor supplied some further details in reference to the pro- posed erection,

THE SANITARY COMMITTEE.-THE MEDICAL .OFFICER AND PRIVATE PRACTICE.

The minutes of this committee stated that the follow- ing letter had been received from the medical officer of health :—Town Hall, Warrington, 28th April, 1888. Dear Sir,—l have now held the appointment of Medical Superintendent, of the Fever Hospital nearly eleven years, and those of Medieal Officer of Health and Public Analyst above eight years. I accepted these posts upon the understanding that I should relinquish private prac- tice, and I have faithfully kept to this agreement. With a view to keeping up my experience as a medical prac- titioner, and of increasing to some small extent my pro- fessional income, I beg to ask your committee to allow me to exercise a small amount of private practice, assur- ing you that I will not let it in any way interfere with my duties as a public officer, and your servant. I remain, yours respectfully, John H. Gornall. John Burgess, Esq. Y.P., Chairman of the Sanitary Committee.—By a reso- lution also recorded, the committee acceded to the above request.—The committee recommended that the tender of Mr. Stephen Moss to supply 200 pairs of pail handles at 3id per pair, and the tender of Mr. C. Cotton to supply the same quantity at the same price, be accepted. Alderman Beeness moved the confirmation of these minutes. Councillor WRIGHT seconded. Councillor PLarr said he did not quite approve of the resolution that the request of the Medical Officer be ac- ceded to, and that he be allowed to exercise private prac- tice. He happened to be a member of the Council when the matter of private practice on the part of the officials of the Ilorougb was Very extensively ventilated. It was well thrashed out at the time of the late Borough Sur- veyor, and the Council was almost unanimous that the System of a Corporation official having private practice in addition to his ordinary duties was not one to be en- couraged ; but, on the contrwy, that it was productive of evil. (Hear, hear.) It would have been as well if the committee had defined, what was meant by private practice—whether it meant one, two, or twenty patient. He could not help thinking that on principle private practice ought not to be encouraged; as other officials of the Corporation might wish to have the same privilege extended to them. There was another point. It would not be advisable for Dr. Gornall to be in the Infectious Diseases Hospital for two or three hours, mix with ' patients suffering from infectious diseases: and after- wards engage in private practice, which might possibly lead to an extension of the very evil the Medical Officer was appointed to prevent, namely, the spread of disease. He moved, as an amendment "That the resolution of the committee approving of the request of the Medical Offi- cer be referred back to the committee for further con- sideration, either to define exactly its terms or otherwise as they may think desirable." Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT seconded.

Alderman HARRISON referred to the salary of the Medi- cal Officer, and said that no medical man under the cir- cumstances would think of devoting the whole of his time to the duties of such an office, and unless they did what the committee suggested they would have to in- crease the doctor's salary. Councillor MONKS had had sufficient experience in the working of private practice to condemn it utterly. He knew that it was the opinion of the Sanitary Committee, when they appointed Dr. Gornall, that private practice had worked very badly, and that they would have no more of it; in fact, that was one of the reasons for the appointment of Dr. Gonaall. He did not see how they could withhold private practice from any other servant if allowed the Medical Officer of Health. The salary was, he believed, about £2OO a year. Alderman HARRISON: £lOO. The DEPUTY MAYOR : £l.OO as medical officer of health, £5O as public analyst, and £lOO as medical officer of the infectious diseases hospital. Councillor MONKS continuing, said that experience had tended to prove that when a man had private prac- tice his public appointments had been subservient, and he should, therefore, most decidedly vote in favour of the amendment on the grounds he had named. . . .
Alderman HARRISON explained that he had been under the impression that the total amount of Dr. Got=ll's salary was £lOO a year; otherwise he might have quali- fied what he had said.

Alderman BURGESS was somewhat Surprised that an objection had been raised by Councillor Platt, and so very heartily, so exceedingly heartily, seconded by Coun- cillor John Pierpoird, From the way in which Council- lor Pierpoint expressed himself, it appeared he would be delighted at any calamity he could bring about if it had reference to the work of the Sanitary Committee. Confirmed on the motion of Councillor J. PIERPOINT. GAS COMMITTEE.—THE RESIGNATION OF MR. JAMES PATERSON. The minutes of this committee contained a letter from Mr. James Paterson, tendering his resignation of the post of manager of the Gas works. The Committee con- sidered it desirable to retain the services of Mr. Paterson as consulting engineer of the works, and proposed to pay him a salary of £lOO per annum for his services. The committee recommended the appointment of Mr. Wil- liam Spence Haddock, the gas e:sgineer to the Corpora- tion, at a salary increased from £l5O to £3OO per annum. It was also recommended that Mr. Frederick Taylor be I appointed secretary of the works, at a salary increased from £195 to £220; and that Mr. W. S. Howard should give all the assistance in his power to Mr. Haddock; and in consideration of his extra duties have his salary in- creased to £l2O per annum. It was resolved, "That a reserve fund be provided to be applicable from time to time to answer any deficiency at any time happening in the income of the gas undertaking, or to meet any extra- ordinary claim or demand at any time arising agkinst the Corporation in respect of that undertaking, and that the sum of £2,500 be set aside and placed to the credit of the reserve fund." It was further resolved that the sum of £2,300 out of such reserve fund be lent to the Paving and Sewerage Committee at £3 5s per cent, on the security of the land in Wharf Meadow, recently pur- chased by that Committee.

Alderman HOLMES, in proposing the confirmation os the minutes of the committee, said that they had en- deavoured, in the arrangements that they proposed to make, to bring everything before the Council, so that all might be clear and above board.- He apprehended that the Council would join with the ,committee in re- gretting that Mr. Paterson had, by reason of his age, resigned his position. They had expressed their sym- pathy with him, and, he had Bo doubt, the Council would fully endorse that action. Having accepted the resignation, it became the duty of the committee to ap- point a successor to Mr. Paterson. They had no hesi- tation in proposing he appointment a Mr. Haddock, who had been in the service of the Gas Committee for many years. They believed that in appointing him to the post of manager, with the assistance of Mr. Patter- son, whose services they, proposed to retain in a small degree, the works would be most efficiently carried on, and the interests of the ratepayers most thoroughly con- sidered. He believed that there was an idea abroad that in proposing the remuneration of £lOO a year to Mr. Paterson a pension was really being proposed. He wished members of the bouncil to entirely disposses their minds of any such idea. If they would look at the wording of the committee's report they would see it stated that Mr. Paterson would attend at the gas works as often as might be nerassary, and that he would be at the services of the committee for consultation and advice so long as it might be deemed advisable that the arrangement should continue. The arrangement was one that might be broken at any time. Mr. Taylor, who had been appointed secretary, was considered thoroughly efficient. They were also asking Mr. Howard to give the manager occasioftal assistance, but they do not propose to add any person to the staff. The expenses of the management had been £1,248 a year, and it was-new-proposed that the work should be done for £1,039, so that the arrangement would effect a saving of over £2OO a year. With regard to the regolu- tion that the sumsof £2,500 te placed to the credit of the reserve fund Alderman Holmes said that it was con- sidered needful that the Gas Committee should lay aside 5. sum of about £lO,OOO, with a view to paying for any loss that might occur in the future. Now that they were able to borrow money at a less rate of interest the amount of their securities went higher, and the payments they had to make to bondholders would probably go up to 27 or 28 years' purchase, or possibly more. It was neces- sary to set aside a sum of money to pay any loss that might occur in that way. Councillor WeiGuir seconded the proposition. Councillor Mosres asked what loss Alderman Holmes referred to. Alderman HOLMES said that on the purchase of the gas works they agreed to give the owners £2 annually for each of their shares, and there were also the perpetual annuities of 14s per share. From time to time they had' endeavoured to buy these annuities up. By an Act of rarliament they were empowered to give 25 years' pur- chase for those annuities. The rate of interest had come down materially, and therefore a perfect security like that was worth more than 25years' purchase now. They would therefpre have to pay more money for the annui- ties, and it was advisable to set apart a sum of money out of which to pay it. Councillor FLEMING asked if the proposed salary of £3OO a year to Mr. Haddock was to be permanent? Would they afterwards be asked to increase it. COURCMOT BOLTON said that he had no objection to Mr. Paterson having £lOO a year,but he thought that in that case the salary of £3OO a year was too much for Mr. ' Haddock. It either meant that Mr. Haddock was not quite qualified and needed supervision, or, that if he was qualified, and deserved £3OO a year, the services of 'Mr. Paterson were not required. Councillor IT. RonaTs'proposed as an amendment "That the consideration of the report of the Gas Committee be deferred until the next ordinary meeting of the Council, and that the Gas Committee be requested in the mean- time to furnish the Council with full particulars of • the duties of the gas manager and secretary respectively, as recently defieed, in order that the same may be discussed together with the report as already published." He did not think that the Connell should be asked to give an opinion on a matter of such importance without having further information. It would be a serious matter to appoint Mr. Haddock without knowing the exact terms ok his engagement. He should like to know whether the important question of private prac- tice was in any way referred to in regard to Mr. Haddock's appointment. If so he should like to know what the terms were. He had heard in an undefined sort of way that he was not to be allowed to receive any perquisities. He should think not—no honest man holding- an official position of that kind needed to be told that he should have no perquisi- tes, when he was supposed to devote the whole of his time to the interests of the Corporation. There was another way in which private practise might be indulged in that was not quite clearly defined. He should con- sider that if a man had a right to take articled pupils at a premium that was tantamount to allow- ing him private practise. The late manager had had a salary of £5OO a year, and also private practise' as a consulting engineer. (" No.") If not, there had been a comparatively recent alteration. He was decidedly of opinion that for some time Mr. Paterson was allowed private practise as a consulting engineer. He had also received considerable remunera- tion in the shape of premiums for articled pupils. At any rate, the person now proposed as manager had paid him a considerable sum for the very purpose, and there might have been others besides. If they proposed to allow the new manager to practically increase his salary by private practise— Alderman Holmes Nothing of that sort is contem- plated ; it is expressly prohibited. Councillor H. ROBERTS said that he had in his posses- sion a printed copy of the suggested duties of the new gas manager. In clause 23 occurred the following words— "To undertake not to actept any perquisite or receive any commission, or other profit of any kind, in respect of any contracts, 'sales, or purchases entered into by the Corporation, or without the sanction of the e,omnaittee to engage any articled pupil, or receive any premium." If there was no contemplation of private practise, why in- sert at all the words regarding the sanction of the com- mittee ?I As a primary condition of his employment why not state distinctly and emphatically at once that he should receive no premiuns for pupils? The clause gave the committee the option to sanction the manager having such a perquisite. Councillor Dixosr, in seconding the amendment, said that the report of the committee was not a very satis- factory one. ALDERMAN BURaSS hoped that the Gas Committee would accede to this request. It would do no harm, and Would give the members of the Council time to think over the matter. With the permission of Mr. Roberts he should like to add an additional request—that the Coun- cil be furnished with the particulars of the leakage dur- ing the last three years, and what such leakage had cost. He was told that the leakage was exceedingly serious, and that .the attention of the Committee should be turned to it with a view of minimising the loss. He should also , like to know how much money had been spent by the Corporation in the purchase of gas annuities. Councillor J. SHAW GREEN said that he thought that'

the chairman of the Gas Committee would also-give them a little further information respecting the financial con- dition of the gas department it wouldpe well. When a financial proposal of these dimeqsions was brought for- ward it would be wise to also add some statement about the finances and general condition of the place. Councillor BARRERI: I should like to suggest that Alderman'Burgess gilbs those particulars promised so long in regard to Longford depot at the mem time. Alderman BURGESS: Permit me to say that every pro- mise of figures that has been given, by me with reference to Longford depot has been fulfilled and carried out. Councillor PLarr supported the amendment. In con- sidering a questionOf this kind, various matters had to be looked at, and it was almost impossible .to do it on such short notice as they had had. He should like to suggest that the arrangements with regard to Mr. Pater- son receiving 100 a year, should be a temporary one, for twelve mouths. The tendency for many years past had been that money was continually getting cheaper, and he did not believe that they would ever be able fel buy the annuities under the present arrangement. Sooner or later they would have to get the Act of Parliament al- tend in that particular. He thought that it would be better to invest the money in the open market in buying up bonds. They should put themselves in a position to buy the bonds. % He also mentioned the question of the gas supply to cottages. He thought that the Gas Com- mittee was losing a considerable portion of what might be revenue by, the present prohibitive regulation as to the supply to dottages. Amongst the cottagers paying about 4s or 4s Bd a week rent they would scarcely find one in

ten using gas. This was because the Gas Conaraittee,o sisted upon a deposit, as, he supposed, a security ag,a's, ba-a debts. He thought that they should mako 1111.'1;4 as much gas as they could. , The regulation prolli,'- cottagers using gas was a matter that demanded sc•-• attention. - tJ Alderman HOLMBS, in reply, offered no objection to, , consideration of the question being adjourned 1.01 moath. One objection to the supply of gas to co- was that some tenants were never in the houses for, b- together, and there was great risk of makinF bad 11,ie which it was important that the committee shotil'-`_, incur. A member wished to know whether the salal.; £3OO was to be a permanent one. He could not all3t for what would happen that day twelve months, b,„`l was in the minds of the committee to fix the sala," such a figure that it would make Mr. Haddock itt„,aer dent, and that he would not require another increa-s°4 some time to come. 'ln answer to a farther que% Alderman Holmes said that in round figures the Pr) of the Gas Committee during the past twelve months, been £12,200; and the payments made to the Cog,' tion for sundry purposes were rather under £9,ouvi, that there was the difference between these two am°, out of which they were able very easily to pal £2,500. The Gas Committee believed it would be the interest of the Corporation to do what was posed. A RIGHT OF WAY QUESTION AT BURTONWOOD.

At the County Petty Sessions, at Warrington, on Wednesday, before Messrs. Edward Greeuall and James Tinsley, Henry Horsley- and Peter Reyes, colliers, were charged with having trespassed on land belonging t Mr. James Fairclough, in the oc- cupation of Mr. Henry Gilroy, and with having done wilful damage to the amount of one penny. Hors- ley was fUrther charged with breaking a fence and thus doing damage to the extent of 10s. Mr. Percy Davies prosecuted, and Mr. H. L. Riley represented the defendants. It appeared from the evidence that the complainant, Mr. Gilroy, occupied a farm, the front of which faced the highroad between St. Helens and Warrington. Between the edge of this farm and a nursery, occupied by Mr. Boardman, there is an opening which leads to the farm, and is continued as a cart road along the fields until it ter- minates at the edge of Sutton Moss, where there is a wide and deep ditch made by Messrs. Evans & Co. This road has been used for some considerable time by the colliers at the Collins Green Colliery as a short cut to their work. Some time ago a gate was placed across the cartway, about nine or ten yards from the highroad. Until lately, this gate was closed with a simple catch. On the 14th of May, about half-past five in the morning, a number of colliers, among whom were Horsley and Reyes, on intending to go along the cartway and across the Moss to their work, found the gate locked and the cart road ploughed up and sown with oats. Mr. Gilroy, who was in the field, warned them to go by the high- road, but Horsley said, "I have the tool for the job," and knocked down the palings on one side of the gate with his pick, and, telling his companions not to touch the planks, walked over the space and over the ploughed land which had been the cartway. Since the summons the men had trespassed as much as even, The defence was that before the present cartway was made, there was a path in its place, which was used by the public, and especially by the colliers. Two witnesses were called who stated that they had used the road, and seen it used by other peoplg, 60 years and 45 years ago respectively. The magistrates decided that tile raising of the question of the right of way placed the case out of their jurisdiction, and it was therefore dismissed.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at the Union Work- house,'Whiston, on Thursday afternoon, when there were present Messrs. J. Kenwright (chairman), W. Middle- hurst, W. Twist, J. Burehall, W. Tyrer C. B. Johnson, J. Birchall, E. Syder, T. Eatook, J. Fisher, J. Musson R. A. Graves, W. R. Longton. W. Daine, H. Hulme, J. Ranson, J. Leatherbarrow, W. Swift, J. Lowe, andS. H. _

Hartley (clerk). RELIES'.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 488 inmates this week, 495 last week, and 470 in the cor- responding week last year; 93 vagrants had beenrelieved, against 88 last year. THE UNION FIRE ENGINF.—The master also asked tl Guardians to fix a charge tor the use of the new steam fire engine when called to a fire in the neighbourhood.— The Clerk stated that the Corporation of St. Helens charged £2 2s Od per hour for the use of their engine, also for horse hire. They further charged 43 for the first hour and 2s per subsequent hour for the services of the superintendent; 3s'for the first hour and is for each subsequent hour for the foreman; and 2s for the first hour and is for each subsequent hour in the case of ordinary firemen. He thought they were reasonable charges and the Guardians ought to make the same. The Fire Insurance Company's would no doubt pay the charges in case of a fire, but the Workhouse Master would have to be fortified with a resolution of the Gnar- dians.—Mr. Fisher nioved that the scale of charges te the same as that at St. Helens, Mr. Lowe seconded ; the motion was adopted.—The Clerk also reported that the Workhouse Master wished the permission of the Guar- dians for the brigade to attend the annual demonstration of Lancashire Fire Brigades at Ashton-under-Lyne. The men had got their new clothing and boots and would make a good show.—Mr. Johnson asked if' the couplings got by the Guardians would work with the mains la( - longing to the Prescot Local Board.—The Clerk stated that he had communicated with the Prescot Local Board and had offered to lend them their engine if they would pay the charges, but he had not received an an- swer .—The matter then dropped, and it was understood that the brigade would be allowed to attend at Ashton- under-Lyne. AUDIT.—Mr. George Ha.zlehurst, the district Govern- ment auditor, wrote that he would audit the accounts of the Board and of the Rural Sanitary Authority on the

18th inst. THE CHILDREN IN CANADA.—Mr. W. Newsome, of , Eccleston Park, wrote forwarding a copy of a communi- cation he had received from thjßev. Thomas W. Fyles, of Canada, from which it appeared that the children sent out to Camada had not been lOsesight of, and that their welfare was being looked after.—ln reply to Mr. Mid- dlehurst. the Clerk stated that 47 children had been sent out.—The information was considered very satisfacwry, and it was decided to send a copy to the Local Govern- ment Board. THE CLERIC'S OFFICE—The Clerk stated that the con- tractor would soon be prepared to proceed with pulling down the present offices, and he asked what provision the Guardians proposed to make for his (the clerk's) office. He did not think the committee rooms would be suitable, and the alterations would not be completed for six months.—After some discussion it was decided to ; leave the Matter in the hands of the clerk and the work- house master. .

THE COMPENSATION QUESTION. Sir,—" Bellerophon "is the Sancho Panza of your cor- respondents. Like Sancho he is always quoting, and al- most always misapplies his quotations. But on making a comparison between the two there is this to be said in favour of the guzzling, liquor-drinking, unheroical page of Don Quixote that he quotes ~goa sound, healthy Spanish proverbs', which may, at all events, be usefully applied by the reader himself, while, on the other hand, "Bellerophon," as a rule, quotes the merest garbage of literature,—stuff which, as I have said before, all real and discriminating admirers of the writers would wish to have forgotten, and which certainly can do no good to anybody except it be, perhaps to illustrate what poor stuff has at times been put into print. There is that about " Bellerophon " and his quotations which nearly convinces one that there is, after all, something in the doctrine of mental affinities. He evidently goes through books out of which other people would, figuratively speaking, gather pearls and ingots of gold, but he gathers nothing but what is poor, mean, and despicable, the cinders, ashes, and mud. .We have heard of parasites which draw out the noxious juices of what they fix upon; in the same way" Bellerophon" by some mental i process, all his own, sucks out all that s odious and putrescent in the volume he fixes upon, and rejects all that is good and wholesome. When " Bellerophon " comes to define what he means by theft we at once discover that he is afflicted with the mental infirmity for which Lord Bacon prescribes a study of the schoolmen. Bacon says if a man's "wit be not apt to distinguish or find differences let him study the schoolmern." Now, that your correspondent's " wit "is "not apt to distinguish or find differences" is clear from the following sentence in his last letter: "A publican" he says, "or tailor' or cobbler, or even a parson who has bought a living, has acquired a tangible and inalienable right to call it his own and the man or men who by act or deed takes it from him is an unmitigated thief." Here he classes the businesses or "livings" of a publican and. a tailor together as if they were on all fours. Now let us consider how egregiously he fails "to distinguish or find differences" which are as clear as noonday. Suppose for a moment that all the now green meadows of Arpley were covered with houses and densely populated there would here be an excellent opening for a variety of business, amongst others of the tailor and publican. The tailor would straightway, without asking anybody's per- mission, set up shop, and ply his trade, but the publican could not do this. He would have to go to the magis- trates and ask for permission, and the permission, if granted, would only be granted for a single year, to be afterwards withdrawn or continued at the pleasure of the magistrates. Here then is difference number one which "Bellerophon" seems never to have perceived. Then, again, the tailor would have to "work up" er create his business. The very next shop to his own, or the whole street of shops, might be occupied by competi- tors, and whether he secured a " living ' or not, would probably entirely depend upon his own capacity or good fortune. But how is it with the publican? The magis- trates in effect say to him—" We not only grant you permission to endeavour to earn a "living," but we give you a living. We grant you a license because we believe there is a demand and a need for the liquors you will sell i in the locality, and the very fact that there s a demand ensures you a business. More than that, we give you a monoply of your trade in that locality, because no com- petitor can start in opposition to you without our sanc- tion, and the very fact that you are already licensed will 'be an argument with us for not giving another license." Surely, even " Bellerophon " will admit that here is an- other " difference" which entirely destroys his attempted analogy between the business of a publican and a tailor. He will perhaps object that many present-day publi- cans have bought the good-will of the business they carry on from predecessors, just as many tailors have done, and therefore ought not to be deprived of it. This is one of those arguments which only expose the poverty of the case of those who use them. The answer is ob- vious, that all property is sold and transferred subject to the legal conditions on which the property is held. A tailor's business and a publican's business are different in the eyes of the law, as one is subject to a yearly license, and is in other ways restricted, and the other is not. If a man buys a publican's business as he would a tailor's, he is either ignoring or ignorant of circumstances to which he ought to be fully alive, and if he suffer in consequence he has none to blame but himself. There are other arguments and illustrations which , might be used to expose 'Bellerophon's" absurdities, but as a champion of the cause he attempts to defend, he is so feebly inadequate that one almost feels as though one was striving against an unsubstantial phantom. In con- clusion I cannot help saying that he might do worse than try the remedy Lord Bacon prescribes for the peculiar mental weakness under which he labours. Let him cease scavenging in the back slums of poetry, and take to studying "the schoolmen," and he will at least get rid of a debilitating habit.—l am sir,
CADMUS.
Warrington, Juns sth, 1888.

RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Thursday. Mr. James Dobson presided, and there were present 'Messrs. S. Taylor, H. White, J. Pritchard, F. A. Lake, F. Wiswall, Whittaker, P. Smith, J. Meadowcroft, W. Mellor, E. Imison, W. Hankinson, H. J. Grice, W. 11. Linakbr (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), Dr. McDougall (medical •officer), and 31. Barker (surveyor).

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. The medical officer of health reported that during the past month there were 27 deaths, of which three were inquest cases; and represented a death rate for the twelve months of 19.1 of the estimated population, and exclusive of the inquest cases of 16.16 of the estimated population. THE OUTBREAK OF TYPHOID FF:VER. Mr. Meadowcroft moved that the Board resolve itself into committee to consider the letters recently received from the Local Government Board respecting the preva- lence of fever in the town; the report of the medical officer thereon, and the letter of censure from the Local Government Board.—Mr. Imison seconded the motion.— Mr.lightbum moved, and Mr. Grice seconded, that the ''matter be discussed in open Board.—The amendment was carried by ten votes to four.— Mr. Meadowcroft then pointed out that at the last meet- ing of the Board a letter was received from the Local Government Board in which they referred to a report made by the medical officer, and stated that they re- gretted that so many conditions obviously tending to in- jure health and to spread disease were not dealt with before the occurrence of the preventible sickness and deaths recorded in the report. He (Mr. Meadowcroft) termed that a letter of censure, but at the meeting re- ferred to the medical officer made some remarks that did not support the tone of that letter. That gentleman said that at the present time there was not a case of typhoid fever in the district; there was no measles and no scarlet fever. There had not been a death through scarlet fever since 1885, a condition of things that was extremely satisfactory, considering that prior to that time scarlet fever was of almost constant duration in the town. At the present time the health of the town was extremely good, and the town was singularly free from preventible diseases.—After some conversation the report that hed called forth the letter was read. The report stated that the number of deaths registered from fever during the quarter ended the 31st December, 1887, in the Runcorn Urban Sanitary District, amounted to seven. The number of deaths from the same cause in the preceding quarter was three. There were about 51 non-fatal cases making a total of about 62 persons at- tacked in the five months named. The nature of the fever was what is known as typhoid or enteric fever. The first person attacked was supposed to have contrac- ted the disease in Widnes, where he worked as a , labourer. He was removed to the fever hospital. The first death recorded occurred in a back house, off a street that runs parallel witiethe river Mersey. Four persons were subsequently attacked in this locality, and were removed to the Union fever hospital at Dutton. The drainage arrangements of this locality were seriously defective. The gully holes were made of brick and not trapped, and were in close proximity to the doors of the dwellings. These serious defects were made good at once. He had no doubt that the cause of the outbreak in this locality was the free escape of sewer gas into a crowded court, surrounded by high walls, and having large open ashpits to aggravate the evil. The houses were occupied by a low class of labour- ing people and this remark applied to the families who were subsequently attacked, and resided (with the exception of one family) in the street referred to above. In this street no fewer than 19 persons were attacked, and one death occurred. There appears to have been constant inter-communication amongst these families, and it seemed probable that the germs of the disease were conveyed by well meaning people into each other's houses, as well as carrying the disease away with them. The majority of the remaining cases were isolated outbreaks, occurring in ten or eleven households and in his opinion the outbreak in each case was directly trace- able to the defective trapping of cellar drains, to the defective construction of some of the yard and house drains, and in one or two instances to their nearness to living rooms, with the natural result that large volumes of sewer gas found ready access into the dwellings. The doctor described the means adopted for stamping out the disease, which was successfully accomplished at the end of December. Mr. Hankinson said the report was a fair and candid one, and proved that the Health Committee acted promptly and efficiently.—Mr. Meadowcroft said the censure of the Local Government Board was not justified by the fact—Mr. Lightbum said the committee had acted with vigilance and vigour in stamping out the dis- ease, and the letter sent by the Local Government Board might have been addressed to any other Authority. It was ultimately resolved that the Health Committee should reply to the letter and repudiate the insinuations contained therein. 1 Ittenwle MATTERS. The Highway and Buildings Committee recommended that a crossing be constructed opposite St. John's Brow, and that two crossways near the Police Station be re- layed. It was also recommended that the tender of Messrs. Thomas Kirkham and Co., for the flagging of the Market-place, Bridge-st., Wellington-st., and Regent-st. be accepted, and also that firm's tender for the cutting and laying of a sewer in the Holloway; and the tender of Mr. Thomas Norman for the supply of glazed stone- ware socket pipes.—Mr. Taylor moved, and Mr. Grice seconded the confirmation of the minutes.—Mr. Hanldn son pointed out that the Board paid about £6O a year for water, and he inquired whether the water at the foun- tain could not be utilised for watering the streets.—Mr. Taylor said the committee, had considered that matter, and had concluded that it would cost twice £BO to do as Mr. Hankinson suggested. They would require three extra horses.—The minutes passed. NEW CATHOLIC owner!.

A letter was read .frOm the Rev. J. B. Gastaldi, of St. Edward's Roman Catholic Church, in which he asked the Board to pass the plans (enclosed) of a new iron church, proposed to be erected in Irwell-lane.—The plans were passed on the motion of Mr. Lightbuna, seconded by Mr. Grice.

HEALTH COMMITTEE. Mr. Lightbum moved the adoption of the minutes of this committee. He stated that the committee desired to increase the gratuity of the Nuisance Inspector to £lO and he made a motion to that effect. The motion was carried.

FINANCE. The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for the month amounted to £1.51 9s Bd, and recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £313 3s 9d.—Car- ried. This was all the business transacted.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIAISt.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIAISt.

The fortnightly meeting was held 4 Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided. and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. J. Mclnyre, P. Speak- man, H. J. Grice, S. Taylor. E. Aaron, J. Stokes, P. Hall, J. Weir, T. Hewitt, J. W. Lightburn, W. Hewitt, J. Smith, E. A. Wallington, J. Brandreth, G. Priestner, T. Hadfield, W. Clarke, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk.) .

THE WEAVER TRUST AGITATION. The Deputy Clerk said that in response to the Com- missioners of the Board, asking other public bodies in the county to support them in a petition against Mr. Brun- ner's proposal to divert the surplus of the Weaver Trust from the County Funds to Salt Trade ; several letters had been received. Macclesfield Town Council and Board of Guardians; Nantwich Local Board and Altrincham Board of Guardians expressed their willingness to join in the protest. The clerk to the Winsford Local Board replied that the only resolution passed in connection with the letter was that it "should lie on the table." (Laughter.) "It must be obvious," he continued, "that if any district has any claim on any surplus derived from the river Weaver it must be the Northwich and Knutsford districts, whence the whole of the revenue from which the county receives so much benefit is actually derived." (A Member : Very disinterested.) The clerk to the Northwich Local Board rerlied that the communications had been referred to the General Purposes Committee, " who, I may say, are not likely to recommend the Board to support the resolution passed by the Runcorn Guardians." (Laughter.) The General Purposes Committee of Crewe had recom- mended the Town. Council to support the view of the Runcorn Guardians.—The Law Clerk said the Board ought to bring in a petition and recommended these authorities to send it up to London in conjunction with themselves.—Mr. Hadfield moved and the Rev. J. Lock- wood seconded a motion that the deputy-clerk prepare a draft petition and submit it at the next meeting.—Mr. P. Speakman said Mr. Brunner, according to the question he asked in the House of dommons appeared to desire a fresh constitution for the Weaver Trust on the lines of the Mersey Docks and Harbeur Board and that the tolls from the Weaver should be devoted not to the alleviation of the area of Cheshire, but, of the salt trade in particu- lar. Since the subject had been raised he (Mr. Speakman) had spoken to some of the largest salt manufacturers, and he found that there was a concensus of opinion that no good at all would be gained by a change. Before Runcorn Bridge was made, salt came down the river Weaver for Wichies and St. Helens, and partly benefited Cheshire and partly Lancashire. Now from 80 to 90 per cent. of the salt used at these places was sent by train across the bridge. Nearly the whole of the salt that now came down the Weaver went to America, India. and other foreign places; and if the salt trade was in the broken up condition it was repre- sented to be, and the salt proprietors at the present mo- ment had the extra shilling toll, it would not benefit Cheshire in the slightest degree, but the advantage ' would accrue to India and other places. He was of opinion that anything that affected the revenue of the Weaver would be most injurious to the interests of Che- shire.—Mr. Hadfield: In other words, whatever reduc- tion of tolls the salt trade might obtain, they would throw the advantage away by cutting each others throats like they do now, and winch is the cause of the depres- sion in the salt trade.—Mr. Speakman: Yes.—The mo- tion was carried.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 9, 1888. SMALLPDX AT WARRINGTON. I MR. MOSS, M.P., AND COMPENSATION.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 9, 1888. SMALLPDX AT WARRINGTON. I MR. MOSS, M.P., AND COMPENSATION.

Master (Mr. Cunnah) said he had pleasure in reporting that the sum of £7 18s eid had been subscribed as fol- lows :—Mr C Reynolds, Frodsham, £1; Mr H Cox, Dutton Lodge, £1; Mr E A Wright, Frodsham, £1; Mr S B Chadwick, Runcorn, £1 is; Mr J 13rundrit, Run- corn, £1; Mr and Mrs Marsden, Aston. £1; Mr A Thomas, Frodsham, lOs ; Mr J Robinson, Frodsham, ss; Mr J Simpson, Dunsdale, as 6cl; and also Messrs G Ward, F W Dunsford, T Riley, and WR de Prez, 2s 6d each. The Master said it would require £lO to give the children a proper treat. A collection was then taken amongst the Guardians present, and £2 34 Old was realised.

A case of small-pox was reported to the Medical Officer for Warrington (Dr. Gornall), on Monday night, by Dr. Williamson, of Lymm, who is the medical officer for the Lymm section of the Man- chester Ship Canal Works. The sufferer is a navvy employed on the works at Thelwall. He left Pres- ton on Friday, the 25th of May. and went to Goose Green, near Wigan, where he 'remained until the following Sunday. He then walked from Goose Green to Latchford, where he took lodgings at 253, Mersey-view. He commenced work on the Monday. and remained at his employment until Friday in last week, when he com- plained of feeling ill, and unfit for work. On the Sunday, however, he was able to walk to Lymm and back to see the doctor. The disease was not recognised until Sunday, when it was duly reported. The patient was immediately removed to the Fever Hospital. Every precaution has been taken by disinfection of the premises, and re-vacci- nation of the adult members of the family with whom he had been residing, to arrest any further spread of the dreaded disease. The young man is a native of Westmoreland. He had not been vaccinated, and the disease is likely to run a severe course, though at present the symptons are favour- able.

In acknowledging a petition from the Good Tern- piers of Widnes against the compensation clauses of the Local Government Bill, Mr. T. C. Edwards- Moss, M.P., writes as follows : House of Commons, 6th June, 1888. Dear Sir,—Your letter was forwarded to me in the North of Scotland and reached me last week. The Petition which you enclosed, I presented to the House of Commons on Monday, accompanied as it is by others of a similar nature from other influential bodies of my constituents. I should much like to be able to support it, but I cannot persuade myself that it would be just or fair to deprive an honest tradesman of his business, which he has carried on in a perfectly legal manner, without granting him compensation, however much one may think that his business is not for the public good. I trust that the proposals as to the method of compensation will be to a certain extent modified before the Bill becomes law. The resolution which you have forwarded to me will have my careful consideration. If I can see my way to meeting some of the points raised in it, while still adhering to the position I have taken up oa this question I need hardly tell you that I shall be very glad to do so —lam, yours faith- fully, _ _ _
T. C. EDWARDS•MOSS.

- . John Thompson, Esq. Several members of the "Hope of Appleton" Lodge, 1.0.G.T., wrote to Mr. Moss asking him to vote against the.compensation clauses, and Mr. Isaac Corns, of Witt- road, has received a somewhat similar reply, Mr. Moss adding that, before he became member for Widnes, he made it known that he was in favour of compensation to publicans.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Work- house on Tuesday. Colonel A.hton presided, and there were present the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. J. Mclntyre. T. Hadfield, J. Brandreth, E. A. Walling- ton, G. Priestner. E. Aaron, P. Hall, T. Hewitt, W. Hewitt, J. Stokes, J. Smith, H. Linker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer), and Mr. J. Farrington (nuisance inspector).

DANGEROUS BUILDING AT HALTON. The Rev. J. Lockwood called • the attention of the Authority to a nuisance which had long existed at Hal- ton. It was that old tumble down cottage at the corner of Norton and Northwkh roads in Halton. It was in a condition dangerous both to life and limb, and the won- der to him was that some life had not been lost ere this. Children had been hurt by falling stones and woodwork. —Mr. Aaron: And there have been traps upset there.— The Rev. J. Lockwood said the house had not been in- habited since he was at Halton, and he had been there 13 years. He gave notice that at the next meeting he would move a resolution upon the matter.

div.head: OUTIIitEAIC OF SCARLET kkVt.R.
div.p: OUTIIitEAIC OF SCARLET kkVt.R.

The Medical Officer reported an outbreak of scarlet fever in the township of Sutton. The disease existed both in the village itself, and in the part of the township known as Frodsham Bridge. There were at present five cases known. He could not discover the origin of the first case, but scarlet fever was prevalent in some dis- tricts adjacent to that of the union, and it was highly probable that the infection had been imported. All pos- sible precautions were being taken to prevent extension of the disease, and he hoped they should be able to keep the outbreak within its present limits. He further re- ported an outbreak of scarlet fever at Davenport's cot- tages near London Bridge, Stockton Heath, Appleton. Four cases had come to his knowledge, all children and one death occurred. There were also two eases of dip- theria at Whitley Superior.—Mr. Stokes said there were very severe restrictions with regard to cattle, sheep, and pigs, and he wished to know if the law provided any res- strictions with regard to human beings.--'-Dr. Adams said any person suffering from disease wilfully exposing him- self without proper precautions against the spread of the disease was liable to a heavy penalty. The Clerk said ' that restriction did not prevent healthy people going to I visit their sick friends, and that was how the disease was spread.—On the motion of Mr. Wallington, seconded by Mr. Aaron, it was resolved that handbills, drawing ' attention to the penalty to which people were liable who wilfully exposed children suffering from infectious disease, should be printed and circulated in the infected districts.—lnspector Farrington said scarlet fever and other infectious diseases were generally spread broadcast from the schools, and it was decided to write to each schoolmaster and schoolmistress in the Union and ask them not to take in children who had beensuffering from infectious disease unless a doctor's certificate was pro- duced.

div.head: SHIP CANAL HUTS,
div.p: SHIP CANAL HUTS,

The Inspector reported that since last meeting he had submitted to the public analyst a sample of water taken from a well sunk to eight huts situated off Moss Side-lane Moore. The analyst certified "This is not a good water, and I cannot recommend it for domestic use. This water was in a broken bottle with an old cork, and very likely the imported matter came from the old cork." The Inspector described the very particular precautions he had taken in getting the sample of water, and differed from the opinion expressed by the analyst. When the well was sunk there was water to the depth of 6 feet, but when he took the sample the water was only about 2 feet. He was sure the water had drained off into the Ship Canal cutting. He suggested that the well should be sunk deeper. The Inspector was instructed to inform Mr. Walker that the Authority could not grant a certi- ficate of occupation upon the analysis before them, and suggest that the well be sunk deeper.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. Mr. James Pritchard occupied the chair, and there were present the Rev. Dr. Gas tilde, Dr. McDougall, Mr. L. C. Beckett, and Mr. G. Moss (clerk).
SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

The Atten-cl-Q-e-CoWiTnitTee-li-el-ci-a--iiiee—tgig on the 29th May, when 23 parents appeared to explain why their children did not attend school regularly. The clerk was ordered to take magisterial proceedings against 13 per- sons and convictions were recorded in each instance. At a subsequent meeting the committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £69 us lid. The report of the attendance officerswere read andconsidered satisfactory, as they showed an increase as compared with the corresponding month last year. There was an increase of 52 on the number on the roll, of 164 in the average attendance, and of three in the per centage. Messrs. Beckett, McDougall, and Lake were appointed a sub-committee for the management of Greenwav-road schools, and the Rev. Dr. Oastilda and Messrs. Imison and Frith were appointed a sub-committee for the management of Mill-brow schools.- Miss Sowerbutts on the 23rd May placed her resignation as bead mistress of the Greenwav-road Board schools in the hands of the committee. the resignation was accepted, and it was decided to advertise for a successor.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.
The Clerk reported that the school fees received during the past month amounted to £l6 16s 4d, and there was a balance of £22 3s 10d in the bank.

INDCSTRIAL SCHOOLS. The Clerk stated that according to custom it would be necessary to pass a resolution "that a sum not exceed- ing £5O be contributed towards the maintenance of children in certified industrial schools during the current year. At the present time there was one boy in Bishop Brown's School and another in Stockport Industrial School. The total cost was £l3 a year. A few weeks ago, a youth who had been discharged from an indus- trial school, called upon him (Mr. -Moss) because his home was not very creditable and he could not obtain any work. He (Mr. Moss) had not seen the boy since.— Dr. McDougall remarked that he attended a levee at the Petty Sessions on Monday last, and was very sorry to see a youth who had been sent to an industrial school fined Ss and costs for being drunk. He thought the Board ought to take an interest in these boys while in school, and ought to receive a statement periodically as to hcw they were individw-ly progressing in their edu- cation; industrial and otherwise.—Mr. Beckett said the benefit received by the boys depended upon how long they were in the industrial school. They were sent there because they were incorrigible.—Dr. McDougall said that there were incorrigibles, but in many instances childrenwere sent because the parents were so thoroughly neglectful, and were short of every attribute of a parent.—The Chairmkn mentioned an in- stance where a boy had been taught a useful trade in the industrial school, and had since done well.—Dr. Mc- Dougall moved the adoption of the resolution moved by the clerk, and urged that the Board should exercise some over- sight over the childrenwhilstinanindustrial school.—Mr. Beckett seconded the motion, and said it would be to the credit and dignity of the Board if they saw that the chil- dren were taught suitable trades for which they had a special liking.—The motionwas carried.—Dr. McDougall proposed that the clerk write to the different schools at which the Board had boys at the present time and ask them to render a statement as to the conduct of the boys, their progress, and their future prospects; also that the clerk pay a surprise visit to the schools at some time or other, and ascertain personally whether they were being attended to strictly within the meaning of the Industrial Schools Act.—Mr. Beckett seconded.— The Chairman said it might be necessary that an occa- sional visit should be made, but the schools were in- spected and well looked after by Government officials. —Dr. Gastildi thought that any expense beyond paying the terms required was unnecessary, as the childrenwere under Government provision.—After some further con- versation the motion was agreed to.

div.head: PRODS HAM.
div.p: PRODS HAM.

SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.—The annual sermons in behalf of the Trinity Wesleyan St n lay School were preached in the Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, on Sunday, by the Rev. Edwin Mosscrop, of North Shields. In the afternoon a special service was conducted for scholars, teachers, parents, and friends by the Rev. A P. Watson, of Runcorn, and was in part a flower service, the chil- dren and their friends having brought with them flowers, which were tastefully arranged on tables in the com- munion and have since been distributed in the neigh- bourhood. The collections at the three services realised £2o3s.

_ RECHABITE DEMONSTRATION AT NORLEY. —The annual Rechabite Festival was celebrated in this village on Tues- day afternoon. when the members of the "Tent "—con- sisting of adults, male and female, and the juveniles— started in procession from the Temperance Hall, headed by the Norley and Overton brass bands. The route taken by the processionists was somewhat longer than on pre- vious festivals. Halts were 'made 'at all the principal residences, of patrons, in the neighbourhood, after which the members returned io the Temperance Hall, where a substantial tea was provided for them. The rest of the evening was spent in various games, and in patronising the different attractions offered in the shape of the usual "fun of the fair." The band also at inter- vals throughout the evening, rendered selections of music.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF Mit. L. CROSBY, OF RUNCORN.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF Mit. L. CROSBY, OF RUNCORN.

A marriage in which much interest was mani- fested took place at Runcorn Parish Church on Thursday morning. The bridegroom was Mr. Leonard Crosby, third son of Mr. Samuel Crosby, of Lainster Gardens, and the bride was Miss Annie Collier, daughter of the late Mr. Samuel Collier, of Run- corn. The bride, who was charmingly attired, car- ried an exquisite bouquet of flowers, and was adorned with a gold brooch, with diamond setting, the gift of the bridegroom. She was attended by Miss Jessie T. Crosby and Miss Edith Crosby, sisters of the bridegroom, who officiated as bridesmaids. They each wore a silver bracelet, and carried a beautiful bouquet of flowers, the gifts of the bridegroom. Mr. William T. Crosby acted as best man. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, vicar, and the bride was given away by her eldest brother, the Rev. S. F. Collier. of Manchester. Afterwards the guests partook of breakfast, and the happy couple re- c.Avedthe congratulations of their numerous friends. During the day Mr. and Mrs. Crosby departed for North Wales, where they will spend their honeymoon, and will subsequently take up their residence in Warrington. The following is a list of the presents :—Rev. S. F. Collier, portraits of the bride's father and mother; Mrs. Collier, feather bed, &c. ; Mr. W. Collier, cheque; Mrs. F. Savage. of Worcester, silver egg stand; Mr. and Mrs. Crosby, family Bible; Mr. H. 0. Crosby, of Manchester, salad bowl; Mr. and Mrs. J. R. Crosby, Man- chester, silver biscuit barrel; Messrs. W. and A. Crosby, carvers; friends at the Warrington Conservative Club, cigar case and pipe; Miss Crosby, butter knife; Miss E. Crosby, dinner gong ; Miss Manney,. Manchester, table cloth; Mr. and Mrs. J. H. Johnson, Silverdale, Carnforth, screen ; Miss E. Savage, inkstand; Mr. A. B. Frith, silver butter knife ; Mrs. Lydiatt, pair of pockets; Mr Steele, white counterpane ' • Mr Jones, Chester, silk umbrella; Mrs and Miss Wood, pair of ornaments; Mr Dawson, three ornaments ; Messrs H Chadwick and J Buckley, coffee pot, jugs, and orna- ments ; Miss Basnett, toilet set; Mr J R Chadwick, silver breakfast cruet; Miss Esther Dawson, bread plate; Miss Emily Withington, pair of brackets; the bridegroom, gold brooch with diamond setting and bouquet; the, bridesmaids each a silver bracelet and bouquet.

div.head: MANCHESTER MURDER.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER MURDER.

The police have as yet no trustworthy tidings of the whereabouts of the convict murderer, Jackson or Firth. Much speculation has been excited in London by vague reports, circulated most probably by inventive correspondents, that Firth had been seen in "several quarters" of the metropolis. One man who went in a mysterious manner into a pub- lic-house and carried out a class of beer to a person outside who was said to resemble Firth, would have been under suspicion if he could have been found, but lie had vanished into space in company with his thirsty companion. The stories that Firth was "making his way to the Continent" and that the London stations were being" carefully watched" are no.doubt_due_to the same hand.

A Bradford contemporary says :—The growing belief amongst many people in Birstall that Charles W. Firth is not Jackson, the Strangeways murderer, does not appear to be shared by the Manchester police. Detective Caminada has been down to Bir- stall, and it is understood that, added to the pub- lished portrait and description of Firth, confirma- tion of kis identity with Jackson has been deduced from a likeness which prevails among the criminal's brothers. The third son of Mr. Firth is said to bear a very striking resemblance to the escaped convict. The police force has to some extent been diminished hut notwithstanding this, the house of Mr. Firth in Station-road is being constantly watched. Another find of prison clothing has been made at the house of Captain Wood, Cromwell-st., Oldham, where a prison sock was found, identified belonging to the Strange- ways murderer, Jackson. Wood is leaving Oldham, and on Wednesday, in removing a bed which had not been used, found a prison shirt between the flock bed and the mattress. He handed it over to the Oldham police, who forwarded it to Manchester for identification. This seems to prove beyond doubt that Jackson went to Old- ham.
A tramping tinman has informed the Horneastie police that he has seen Firth at Coningsby, a village eight miles away. Inquiries are being made to verify the man's statement.

The Italian Consul at Zanzibar has hauled down his flag, and broken off relations with the Sultan, who has refused, it is said, to carry out an agreement made by his predecessor relative to the cession of certain territory to Italy. MR. MORLEY ON IRELAND.—Mr. John Morley was the principal speaker at a meeting on Thursday night of the London Liberal and Radical Union called to condemn the Irish policy of the Government. Nobody could say that the desire for Home Rule in Ireland was one whit less ac- tive than it was two years ago, or that one constituency in Ireland had chang,ed its mind upon this great issue. If the object of the promoters and promulgators of the Papal Rescrint was to draw away the national clergy from the national movement in Ireland, never did men make a greater mistake. The right honourable gentleman went on to examine the administration of the Crimes Act, and to criticise some of Mr. Balfour's inaccurate statements on the sub- ject: and he asserted that an increase of sentence in al criminal ease on appeal never did happen in England, and had been declared by some of the highest legal , authorities not to be legal. He contended that the words used by the magistrate who passed sentence on Mr. Dillon, to the effect that that gentleman's language had great influence upon the people, proved that the , Irish members were being imprisoned as political leaders; ' and he concluded by making an appeal to the people of , the metropolis to help to remove the stigma resting upon this country. He felt sure, he said, that the system of coercion would soon be swept away, and that those responsible for it would be consigned to the wilderness.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (omtinated from page 6.)
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (omtinated from page 6.)

WESTON. Notwithstanding the inconvenient interference of the Mersey Conservancy Board with the construction of the landing stage at Frodsham, work has been actively pur- sued during the past week. The navvies have been busily engaged in preparing the land for the advent of the more powerful machinery, and in laying a bank be- tween the waters of the river and the proposed cutting. More important matters may have to be chronicled in a few days. _ _

RUNCORN. There is nothing fresh to report this week. The vigi- lant activity in the removal of the soil is still continued, and the spoil bank at Norton becomes visibly larger day by day. The cutting from the depot at Norton now ex- tends to a point opposite the tannery of Messrs. Rey- nolds, and in a few weeks will join the cutting commen- cing above the works of Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele. In about five weeks Mr. Gregson, the energetic agent, expects that the steam navvies under his charge will be breaking up the land near the Old Quay Docks.
LYMM.

At Statham the canal -contractor hag erected one of Murray's patent brickmaking machines, said to be capa- ble of turning out 32,000 bricks a day. The clay, a bed of whieth has been struck upon at this locality, is of a very suitable sort for brick-making. The plant is al- ready in full working, the raw material being carried up to the brick-making machine in wagons drawn by loco- motives. The field is capable of turning out 200,000 bricks weekly, and it is said that it is proposed to make about 20,006,000 bricks to be used in connection with the canal. The steam navvies have not yet been put in operation at Statham, but work is vigorously carried on by hand labour. Another and heavier locomotive, named the "Lancaster," has been brought on the ground. Under the weight of this locomotive the bridge over the river at first showed some signs of yielding, but now seems to have found a solid foundation.

THELWALL. At Morris Brook the new English steam navvy is now in full week and tears up the sandy soil in fine style. Near Thelwall the two other na% nes of the same type are still constantly engaged, but the " Jubilee " navvy seems to have come to grief, and now lies evidently wait- ing for repairs. The Rodley steam navvy was, yester- day, also at a standstill through some mishap we believe A still greater number of workmen are engaged in the excavation of the river bed, and during the Week the means for raising the displaced soil to the top of the spoil heaps have been increased.
